306 GIS Requirements 
The County Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is using GIS 
technology for capturing, managing, analyzing, and displaying all forms of 
geographically referenced data and information. GIS data submitted to the 
County shall comply with the Arizona Spatial Data Accuracy and Geo -
Referencing Standards available from the  Arizona Professional Land 
Surveyors (APLS). Submit GIS information in a geodatabase (.dbo) file for 
raw data and when appropriate a map package (.mpkx) file. 
 
The goals of GIS are:  
1. Coordinate the GIS activities for County departments, 
2. Provide shared services for municipalities, 
3. Promote data standards for the GIS user community in Navajo 
County.  
 
See the County GIS Quick Link for additional information. 
 
307 Improvement Plans 
 
307.1 General 
All improvement plans must comply with the following requirements: 
1. All design must be in accordance with this Manual, Subdivision 
Regulations, Standard Specifications, Standard Details and 
General Notes. 
2. All plans must follow the current Navajo County CAD Standards. 
3. Coordinate new street right -of-way or utility easements with the 
Public Works Department; except if they are in conjunction with a 
subdivision plat in which case, they shall be coordinated through 
Planning & Development Services as part of the subdivision plat 
process. 
4. All water and sewer utility design must be per the latest ADEQ 
requirements and submitted to them for approval. 
5. Design and construct all improvements in accordance with County 
policies, standards, regulations, ordinances, and details.

6. Clearly delineate and identify all relevant jurisdictions and

7. Differentiate between the existing and proposed improvements and

8. Show all utilities identified by a current Arizona 811, certified

on the plans complete with line sizes, types (i.e., water, sewer, gas,

9. Hard copy plan sheets shall be 22” x 34”  in size on good quality

13. All final improvement plans submitted to the County shall be high

Final Plat approval onto plans. 
2. All design must be in accordance with the current Navajo County 
Subdivision Regulations, this Manual, Standard Specifications, 
Standard Details and General Notes. 
3. The improvement plans must include a general master utility layout 
for the subdivision as one of the sheets in the total set of plans. 
4. Comply w ith the County Storm Water Regulations and the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Guidelines for storm water 
discharge. 
5. Small scale subdivision sheet index map (north to top or to right 
side of sheet). 
 
307.3 Cover Sheet 
A Cover Sheet is required for all construction plans submitted. The cover 
sheet includes the following when applicable. 
1. Vicinity Map (including a north arrow). 
2. Project title, Address, and any applicable Navajo Project 
information. 
3. Consultant/Developer names and addresses. 
4. Professional Engineer’s seal and signature. Proper use of 
electronic signature for digital submittals is required. 
5. Signature Block Requirements: 
• Public Improvements: Navajo County Engineer 
6. Block for Arizona Department of Environmental Quality approval 
(file number and date), if applicable. 
7. Completed signature blocks for representatives from all potentially 
affected utility companies. 
8. Applicable Notes. 
9. Index of the sheets. 
10. List of all regulatory agencies which have been notified and/or have 
issued permits.

307.4 General Notes, Quantity, and Index Sheet 
General Notes Sheet shall contain the latest applicable County notes for 
the improvements proposed. See the County Standard Details, 200 
Series. 
 
Quantities Sheet provides a detailed list of quantities broken down by 
sheet. If the project is to be phased, separate quantities must be provided 
for each phase. If the project includes both public and private 
improvements, separate quantities shall be provided accordingly. 
 
Key Index Sheet for improvement plans with more than two (2) sheets, a 
separate key index sheet is required. This sheet shall provide a graphical 
index referencing for all improvement sheets included with the project (i.e., 
paving, storm drain, etc.). 
 
307.5 Horizontal and Vertical Control Sheet 
Horizontal Control Sheet shall include the following: 
1. The origination point of all horizontal position systems shall be 
based on physical survey points or monuments and identified on 
the plans. 
2. Design alignments to proceed from south to north, west to east, left 
to right. 
3. Station all plan sheets in 100-foot intervals at a minimum. 
4. Clearly identify bearing and distance on all horizontal control on 
each sheet. Identify bearing and distances for each change in 
bearing. 
5. Projects will require Temporary Benchmarks (TBM) established by 
a surveyor when it is necessary to maintain vertical control. Vertical 
control shall be per Section 305.2.2. For site plans, establish at 
least three (3) temporary benchmarks (TBM) and shown on the 
plans. For alignment plans (e.g., Roadways, Waterlines, Drainage 
Channels), establish a TBM near the beginning of the project, near 
the end of the project and at lea st every 600 linear feet along the

307.6 Plan and Profile Sheets 
Plan and Profile Sheets shall include the following: 
1. Standard single plan and profile will be required. The County will 
not accept double plan and profile unless approved by the County. 
2. Plans must show sizes, types and locations of all existing and new 
utilities, including services, paving, curb, sidewalk, fire hydrants, 
valves, manholes and all miscellaneous items of construction, such 
as street sign posts, driveways, etc.

6-inch pipe versus proposed 6 -inch pipe) per the most recent 
County CAD Standards.

right side of the sheet, whenever possible. Station storm Drain, 
channel and sewer plans from downstream to upstream, whenever 
possible. 
5. Plan view and profile view must align. 
 
307.7 Detail Sheets 
Detail sheets are supplemental sheets that depict special construction 
details required to clarify some aspect of the proposed improvements. 
 
Do not include County, ADOT, or MAG Standard Details on detail sheets 
unless the detail is modified. Clearly identify modifications to those details 
and include the following text “Modified Navajo County, ADOT, or MAG 
Detail” and include the detail reference number.

309 Construction and Improvement Plan Submittal 
 
309.1 Plan Review 
Prior to issuance of any permit for construction, plans review and approval 
by the County is required. The review is to assure general compliance with 
County Standards, Details and Specifications. 
 
Upon completion of the review, the Professional Engineer will be notified 
by email when to pick up their submittal. 
 
309.2 Plan Review Comments 
Address project plan review comments (including redlines) via correction 
or a clarification response. If there is a discrepancy concerning a redline 
comment, contact the County. Return the redline set of plans with the next 
improvement plan submittal. 
 
Include a separate tabulation of review comments addressing each 
comment and the correction measure provided. The tabulated review 
comments shall depict the comment, comment originator, sheet number 
of the comment, and disposition to the comment. Upon comp letion, 
forward the table to County for review prior to the comment resolution 
meeting. During the comment resolution meeting, final disposition will be 
determined. Subsequent submittals shall then reflect all necessary 
changes as outlined by the direction  in the disposition table. The 
subsequent submittal shall include a copy of the comment disposing table 
and final disposition with a set of the revised documents. 
 
Failure to identify all the changes may result in the return of the plans with 
an additional review required and may require additional review fees 
based on the approved fee schedule.

309.3 General Submittal Requirements 
All submittals should be made  via the County’s MaintStar Permitting 
Center; see Quick Links. Private developers should submit all required 
documents through the MaintStar Permitting Center. 
 
The Consultant/Developer must comply with the following County 
submittal requirements: 
1. A Letter of Transmittal, in duplicate and signed by the Professional 
Engineer, shall accompany all improvement plan submittals. The 
letter of transmittal shall indicate the following: 
• Date of delivery of submittal 
• The review number (1st review, 2nd review, etc.) 
• The number and type of plans which are being submitted 
• The number and type of all required standard forms being 
submitted 
• Engineering permit number 
2. The “red lined” checked prints and checklists from the previous 
review shall accompany all succeeding reviews (no exceptions). 
Likewise, a copy of the preliminary reports and/or studies shall 
accompany submittals of all subsequent reports and/or studies. 
3. The submittal is to include a copy of the project’s 
Geotechnical/Soils Report for County review. Any areas of 
expansive soil may require special treatment during project 
construction. The Professional Engineer shall include any special 
requirements on the plans. 
4. Submit all Private Development plans to Planning & Development 
Services; do not hand -carry any plans to Department Directors or 
Plan Reviewers. Without a copy of the transmittal letter stamped 
“received,” plans are not in the review process. Pay all review fees 
at the time of submittal. 
5. All Private Development projects must include approved 
Preliminary Plat/Site Plan, Drainage Study, a copy of conditions or 
stipulations, Title Report, Schedule B items,  Vesting Deed, and 
other required documents prior to improvement plan submittal.

309.4 Utility Company Approvals 
Local Utility Companies shall sign the cover sheet of construction or 
improvement plans. By signing this sheet, the utility confirms that they 
have seen the plans, are aware of the scope of the project, and have 
identified existing and proposed utilities a nd their potential conflicts in 
relation to the project. 
 
The County shall not approve construction plans until all potentially 
affected utilities have signed or the Professional Engineer has written 
correspondence from each utility confirming no conflicts or resolution of 
conflicts. Utilities which will commonly  be contacted are cable TV, gas, 
electric power, telephone, sewer, and water. 
 
A full set of improvement plans with the “Utility Location and Conflict 
Notice” shall be submitted to each appropriate utility company in parallel 
with each submittal. 
 
309.5 Submittal Deliverables 
 
309.5.1 First Submittal  
Submit all deliverables in PDF format through the MaintStar Permitting 
Center.  
• Construction Plans (Grading, Drainage, Paving, Water, Sewer, 
Streetlight, Traffic Signal/Interconnect, Signing and Striping, 
Landscape, Erosion and Sediment Control, etc.) 
• Final Drainage Report (a complete report, not an addendum to the 
Preliminary Drainage Report). 
• Traffic Impact Analysis or Statement 
• Final Geotechnical/Soils Report  
• Sewer and Water Report 
• Approved Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) – 
Professional Engineer to use standard BMP detail sheet. 
Contractor or Developer will be responsible for obtaining NOI and 
Permit. 
• Engineer’s Opinion of Probable Cost, if applicable  
• Project Specifications  
• Water Provider “Will Serve” letter for private development or 
subdivisions

312.1.2 General Information 
1. Show a complete list of all materials installed and abandoned. 
Show the specific size and material type of each pipeline installed

2. On recorded plat or map of Dedication, show easements and

instruments and described by metes and bounds must be

3. Prints must be blacklines on white background, having dark, clean, 
crisp, clear line work, symbols, and annotation. These items must 
be sufficient boldness and size and be free from background 
obscuring, to be legible and easily read. No shading or tinting is 
acceptable. 
4. Minimum acceptable height for all as-built record drawing lettering 
is 1/8 inch. Larger lettering is preferred, especially for 
dimensioning, stationing, size, material, slope, and elevation 
callouts. Standard bold block lettering is required. 
5. All items changed or unchanged must have a bold (AB) lettered 
next to them. Clearly show required minor as-built changes to the 
approved plans by boldly striking through the item changed and 
placing the as-built information next to or as near as possible to it. 
All as-built annotation changes must be larger and bolder than the 
original and free from background obscuring. 
• Note: This includes abandoned pipe. Abandoned pipe must 
be notated that it is slurry filled, crushed, remained in place, 
or physically removed. 
6. On phased projects, clearly show the phase lines on the key map 
and on the plan and profile sheets and their locations clearly 
identifiable. Show actual pipe end locations relative to phasing lines 
by dimensioning or stationing.

312.1.3 Water Information 
1. The record drawing must indicate the locations of the beginning(s) 
and end(s) of the construction and all valves, fire hydrants, pipe 
fittings and service connections. Show their locations by stationing 
and dimensioning from appropriate monument lines or in their 
absence appropriate lot lines, property lines or easement line 
references. No dimensioning from points of curvature or tangency 
is acceptable for as -built record drawing purposes. The drawings 
must clearly indicate the specific points of reference. 
• Note: In all cases where the pipeline is constructed within or 
parallel, in proximity, with the right-of-way, all stationing and 
dimensioning must be from the nearest appropriate 
monument line and monument line intersection. 
2. The water service stationing shown must be the locations of the 
taps at the main. Measure their locations perpendicular or radial 
relative to the appropriate right -of-way monument line, easement 
centerline, or property line intersection. Indicate service t ap by 
using the following method throughout the plan set. 
• Stationing in the same general direction along a straight or 
curvilinear pipe run starting with the nearest appropriate 
monument line or monument line intersection, or in their 
absence, appropriate easement line references as noted in 
Section 312.1.2, Note 1, as Station 0+00. Show the relative 
stationing of all monument line intersections occurs along 
the pipe runs. When a monument line intersection occurs 
along the pipe run, the service tap stationing should again 
begin with Station 0+00 at the inter section and the process 
repeated to the end of the pipe run. Do not locate 0+00 at 
the closed end of a cul-de-sac or similar type street. 
• Note: When water services are not installed perpendicular 
to the water main, both the location of the tap at the main 
and the distance of the meter set from the nearest side 
property line of the lot must be shown. 
 
312.1.4 Sewer Information 
1. For purposes of the record drawing, every manhole, cleanout, pipe 
plug and building connection tap must be located by stationing 
based upon the nearest downstream manhole always being 
designated as Station 0+00. Cumulative stationing along the length 
of th e pipe run is not acceptable. In addition, the building

Where the building connection service line is not constructed

312.1.5 Cathodic Protection  
Cathodic protection features may appear on either Water or Sewer plans. 
These features include conduit lines, test stations, anodes, and rectifiers. 
Cathodic protection stationing is the same as water stationing when they 
appear on a water plan and the sam e as sewer stationing when they 
appear on a sewer plan as described above. 
 
312.1.6 Asset Management Coordination 
The County requires a CSV file with coordinates ‘X’ (Easting) and ‘Y’ 
(Northing) values which represent the location of certain asset types. 
Coordinates shall comply with Section 312.1.1. For a water system, these 
asset types are fire hydrants, valves, and service lines. For sanitary 
system, these asset types are manholes, cleanouts, and tap laterals. The 
depth from existing or finished grade to top of the asset is required for 
valves, service lines, and tap laterals.  
 
The County may provide an asset management coordination spreadsheet 
during the design phase (stage) that may be used to capture the asset 
coordinate locations as part of the asset management coordination 
process.

312.1.8 Grading, Drainage and Pavement Information 
If applicable, record drawings shall include:

• Finish floor elevations

devices, retention volumes, retention bottoms and top of slopes,

to show direction of the flow.

312.2 Record Drawing Submittal 
Include a Letter of Transmittal to document who is submitting Record 
Drawings. This is necessary in order to process the plans and for contact 
information when the review is complete. Plans will not be reviewed if 
transmittal documentation is missing. 
 
Record Drawings submitted for review shall consist of two (2) electronic 
copies in appropriate digital format as requested by the County, containing 
all the original signatures. 
 
One (1) set will be reviewed and returned if there are County comments. 
All comments must be addressed. Two revised plan sets will be required 
with each resubmittal along with the previous redlined review set until final 
County approval is obtained. 
 
If the project is developed in phases, Record Drawings for each phase 
shall be submitted once the work is complete in that phase. Letters of 
Completion and Acceptance or Certificates of Occupancy will not be 
issued until all items out of tolerance as noted in the walk-through punch-
list have been corrected and all final Record Drawings have been 
submitted and approved by the County.

information provided as a public record.

The County will accept applicable improvements following final inspection, 
approval, and receipt of approved Record Drawings. It is the responsibility 
of the developer, Professional Engineer and contractor to coordinate 
timely submittals of the Record Draw ings in order to affect a Final Letter 
of Completion. 
 
Furthermore, a Final Letter of Completion or Certificate of Occupancy 
shall not be issued to the developer of the project until all affected 
roadways are restored to their previous condition or better and all 
applicable signing and pavement markings have b een installed and 
inspected by the County. All survey monuments shall be installed or 
replaced, if destroyed, before a Final Letter of Completion. 
 
312.3 Results of Survey 
A Registered Land Surveyor shall provide to the County a sealed, Post -
Construction Results of Survey drawing relating to the new, re-established 
or replacement monuments. The Results of Survey shall be recorded with 
the County. 
 
In addition, the surveyor shall complete: 
• Once recorded, submit copies of the documents to Planning & 
Development Services.  
• The survey notes showing these referenced monuments and 
elevations certifications shall be reflected on the as -built 
documents and submitted for approval to the County before the 
project will be accepted as completed or bonds released.  
• Submit all monument information, as referenced above, within 60 
days of County acceptance or Certificates of Occupancies will be

400 Street Transportation Planning 
The intent of this Chapter is to give the references and guidelines for the 
layout of transportation facilities with the County. The designer shall utilize 
the information in the Chapter in conjunction with the other Chapters in 
this Manual. 
 
401 Codes, Standards and Transportation Plans 
The County has the following related transportation planning documents 
available on the Planning & Development Services website: 
• Comprehensive Plan 
• Transportation Plan 
• Area Plans 
 
The County has adopted the Comprehensive Plan, which addresses the 
County’s long -range plans for local and regional transportation 
requirements. The County and a current traffic impact analysis or study 
shall be used to determine the specific roadway requirements.  
  
All street improvements shall be in accordance with the County’s adopted 
Comprehensive Plan and satisfy all required development fees. 
 
402 Federal Functional Classification 
The Federal Functional Classification  (FFC) defines the role that a 
particular roadway segment plays in serving the flow of traffic. Functional 
classes help planners and engineers properly channel transportation 
movements efficiently and cost effectively. Federal funding for road 
development, improvement, or maintenance is tied to functional class.  
 
Use the desired Level of Service (LOS) designations for each roadway 
section in the traffic analysis to support federal function classifications, 
sizing of interim and ultimate roads and determining the number of 
intersection auxiliary lanes. See Table 402.1 for Roadway Section Level 
of Service (LOS) definitions.

Table 402.1 Roadway Section Level of Service (LOS) 
LOS Description 
A Free flow, with low volumes and high speeds. 
B Reasonably free flow, speeds beginning to be restricted by traffic 
conditions. 
C Stable flow zone, most drivers restricted in freedom to select their 
own speed. 
D Approaching unstable flow, drivers have little freedom to 
maneuver. 
E Unstable flow, may be short stoppages. 
F Forced or breakdown flow 
 
These following categories comprise the hierarchy of functional 
classification of roadways in the County and related directly to the different 
types and lengths of generated trips as well as access needs. Travel 
demand determines these characteristics.  
 
Arterials are designed for mobility and allow motorists to travel to their 
destinations at high speeds and with as little delay as possible. Arterials 
are typically used for long distance trips, either across states, counties, or 
large cities and may have up to 3 -lanes in each direction of travel. The 
types of arterial functional classes include: 
• Principal Arterial - Interstate (FFC 1) 
• Principal Arterial - Freeways (FFC 2) 
• Principal Arterial - Other Principal Arterial (FFC 3) 
• Minor Arterial (FFC 4) 
 
Collectors are designed for access and "collect" motorists from local 
roads and connect them to other neighborhoods, businesses, and arterial 
roads. Have at least 1 -lane in each direction of travel. The types of 
collector functional classes include: 
• Major Collector (FFC 5) 
• Minor Collector (FFC 6) 
 
Local Roads (FFC 7) are design to provide the most access to 
neighborhoods but with the least amount of mobility. 
 
Primitive Roads are non-FFC roads and are designed to provide limited 
access with minimal impacts to the surrounding environment.

Subdivision Roads  are non -FFC roads and are designed to provide

402.1 Federal Aid Network 
The Federal Aid Network includes the roads where federal funding is 
available. Funding varies for urban and rural areas. 
 
402.2 Road Classification Considerations 
Mobility versus Access is the most important factor considered when 
classifying a road. 
 
Mobility refers to roads with few opportunities to enter or exit. With limited 
road access, traffic is able to  flow with little friction (i.e. slow down). 
Interstates and freeways, which have ramps controlling access to the 
roads, are the most mobile of the functional classes. 
 
Accessibility refers to roads that have many opportunities to enter or exit 
the road. Accessible roads make it easier to navigate around 
neighborhoods or business districts. However, with more motorists able 
to enter or exit the road, traffic friction increases, which increases the 
chances of traffic jams. Local roads, which allow homeowners to enter 
roads directly from their driveways, are the most accessible functional 
class. 
 
While most roadways offer both “access to property” and “travel mobility” 
services, it is the roadway’s primary purpose that defines the classification 
category to which a given roadway belongs. 
 
Connectivity: With rare exceptions, any road classified above local must 
start and stop with a road that is the same or higher functional class. For 
example, a minor arterial must terminate with another minor arterial or a 
principle arterial but not end with a major collector. 
 
Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT): Measures the traffic volume of a 
road over the course of a year. This value is typically calculated using 
traffic measurement devices, like pneumatic road tubes or piezoelectric 
sensors. If a road is on -the-fence between two functional classes, AADT 
can be useful to decide which functional class is best.

Average Daily Trips (ADT): Measures the number of vehicle trips in both 
directions, measured on a 24-hour basis divided by the number of days in 
the measurement period. ADT may be used when AADT is unavailable in 
deciding which functional class is best. 
 
Major Community Development Changes:  Changes due to recent 
construction of major activity centers (e.g. malls, universities, sport 
venues, hospitals, amusement parks, military bases, other) that would 
create more traffic in an area. 
 
Context: Whether a road is in an urban or rural area may influence its 
functional classification.  
 
Census Data: The 2020 U.S. Census provides the following criteria for 
defining urban and rural areas: 
• Urban Context Areas: Encompass at least 2,000 housing units or 
at least 5,000 people. Urban areas are typically densely developed 
and include residential, commercial, and non-residential land uses. 
• Rural Context Areas: Encompass all population, housing, and 
land not included within any urban areas. 
 
The following Navajo County communities are classified as urban per the 
“List of 2020 Census Urban Areas”: Heber-Overgaard, Pinetop-Lakeside, 
Show Low, Snowflake and Winslow.  
 
It is important to know that, for federal functional classification, local 
agencies may have their own interpretation on whether a road is urban or 
rural, FHWA , ADOT and Navajo County  use U.S. Census data to 
determine a road's urban classification.  Figure 402.1 shows typical 
symbology used on maps, in GIS and this Chapter for Federal Functional 
Classification.

Motorized Operate motorcycles, cars, buses and other transit vehicles,

Bicyclists
 
Typically present in all contexts, although numbers vary. 
Regardless of volumes or location on the facility, the 
safety of bicyclists must remain a high priority. Volumes 
and speeds of motorized vehicles affect the quality of 
service and experience for bicyclists.  
Pedestrians
 
Pedestrians use roadways in all contexts. Even if 
pedestrians are not present throughout the facility or 
volumes are low, their safety and quality of experience 
should remain a high priority. The volumes and speeds of 
motorized vehicles affect pedestrian quality of service. 
Transit 
 
Common feature of suburban, urban, and urban core 
contexts. Coordination with local agencies is imperative 
to discern the potential impacts of transit and ensure 
transit needs are integrated. 
Freight Vehicles include trucks, oversize/overweight vehicles, 
and farm implements or equipment. Trip lengths and 
destinations vary for these users. Freight vehicles may 
pass through a context as part of long-distance service or 
access local commercial, light indu strial, or warehousing 
sites requiring truck deliveries.

402.3 Other Principal Arterials (FFC 3) 
 
 
 Mobility: Connects major activity centers within 
metropolitan areas as well as large cities in rural 
areas. Typically has higher traffic volumes than 
minor arterials.  
   Accessibility: Pedestrian and bicycle opportunities 
are usually present in urban contexts and may be 
limited or missing in rural contexts.  
   
 
Connectivity: Serves specific land parcels directly, 
has at -grade intersections at dispersed locations 
and may have stoplights.  
 
Approximate AADT (Urban): 7,000 to 27,000 
Approximate AADT (Rural): 2,000 to 8,500 
45+ 
MPH 
Speed: Posted speed limits usually range between 
45 mph and 65 mph. 
 
Context 
Urban: Serves as a high -traffic corridor between 
outlying residential neighborhoods and major activity 
centers, including central business districts; 
entertainment districts and venues; air, rail, and bus 
terminals; important recreational areas; regional 
shopping centers; military bases; and more… 
Typically, do not penetrate neighborhoods  & a re 
more spaced apart than Minor Arterials . Desired 
LOS D. 
 Rural: Provides high-speed corridors between large 
cities that have 25,000 people or more. Typically, do 
not penetrate neighborhoods. Roads are continuous 
without dead ends. Desired LOS C.

 Mobility: “Collects” traffic from local roads and steers

MPH

402.6 Minor Collectors (FFC 6) 
 
The following image is an example of a minor collector (FFC 6) in Navajo 
County. 
  
 Mobility: Connects neighborhoods to arterial or major 
collector roads. Trips are typically short distances. 
Serves residential traffic and provides access to local 
businesses. May see little or no through traffic 
movement 
   
Accessibility: Direct access is available from 
neighborhood roads and to adjacent land. Pedestrian 
and bicycle opportunities are usually present in urban 
contexts and may be limited or missing in rural 
contexts.     
 
Connectivity: Residential driveways may attach 
directly to them. Less likely to cross county 
boundaries.

vehicles

402.7 Local Roads (FFC 7) 
 
The majority of  the roads in the County are classified as Local Roads 
(FFC 7). The following images are examples of local roads (FFC 7) in 
Navajo County. 
  
 
Mobility: A neighborhood road that provides 
connectivity to a collector or arterial. Discourage 
through traffic. 
   
Accessibility: Direct access is available from 
adjacent land, businesses, residences and farms. 
Pedestrians and bicycles may have specific facilities, 
such as sidewalks, but may also share the road with 
vehicles.    
 Connectivity: Residential driveways attach directly 
to them. There may be stop sign controlled or 
uncontrolled intersections. Typically, shorter than 
higher classified roads.

Approximate AADT (Rural): 15 to 400

402.8 Roads without Federal Function Classifications 
 
402.8.1 Primitive Roads (NFFC 8.1) 
Per Arizona Revised Statutes (A.R.S.), the Board of Supervisors may 
designate roads meeting specific criteria, set forth in the statutes. Signs 
warning the traveling public must be posted; see Chapter 500. 
 
Primitive roads have the following service characteristics: 
1. Defined by State Statute and established per Resolution. 
2. Limited maintenance is allowed under State Statutes. 
3. Must be reclassified from this designation by the Board of 
Supervisors and brought into the County’s declared roadway 
system before expending public funds for improvements. 
 
402.8.1.1 Eligibility 
Primitive road classification shall apply to public roads meeting all the 
following criteria. 
1. Opened before June 13, 1990 
2. Not constructed in accordance with County standards. 
3. Not a County or State Highway. 
4. Shall have adequate easements dedicated to the public. See Table 
622.1. 
5. Shall be in a condition that the County can grade with minimum 
cost and risk. 
6. Paved roads are not eligible for Primitive Road designation.

402.8.1.2 Functional Classification 
Primitive roads are not classified by functional classification, but by use 
by high-clearance or four-wheel drive vehicles and typically have very low 
traffic volume. The location and design of primitive roads are governed by 
environmental compatibility, expected uses, and minimizing County costs 
with minimal consideration for user comfort or travel time. Typical users 
include dispersed recreation, local access, government, farm, or ranch, or 
administrative. 
 
402.8.1.3 Primitive Road Designation Application Guidelines 
The following items shall accompany any request to designate a road as 
a Primitive Road prior to consideration by the Board of Supervisors. 
Submit all items to the County for review. 
1. An application letter and petition outlining the request for the road 
to be designated as County maintained Primitive Road. 
2. Documentation that the road was opened prior to June 13, 1990. 
3. A map showing the existing location of the road and all properties 
that it traverses. 
4. An easement dedicating the roadway to the public shall be signed 
off by all affected property owners on a form provided by the 
County. 
5. After review of items 1 through 4 above, the County will prepare a 
recommendation for action to the Board of Supervisors.  
6. Upon adoption of the Resolution accepting the grant of the 
Primitive Road easement by the Board of Supervisions, the road 
will be designated as a Primitive Road. 
 
402.8.2 Subdivisions (NFFC 8.2) 
These are typically local roads built to County standards in accordance 
with the subdivision approval process. No ADT requirement is set. 
 
402.8.3 Cul-de-Sacs and Turnarounds 
These are roads where traffic enters and exits at only one end of the road 
and require traffic to turnaround.

403 Street Layout and Planning 
The primary layout for streets is a grid intending to provide public access 
to all legitimate land parcels. The secondary layout for streets is the 
conformance to topographic features and constraints in concert with land 
division boundaries intending to provide public access to legitimate land 
parcels. Streets, lots, tracts, and easement planning and layout shall be 
in accordance with the Subdivision Regulations, Zoning Ordinances, and 
Approved Site Plan.  
 
403.1 Continuation 
Street layouts shall provide for the continuation of existing streets in 
adjacent areas, and such other streets as required by the County. 
 
403.2 Future Street Extensions 
Certain proposed streets, as designated by the County, shall be extended 
to the development boundary to provide future connection with adjoining 
unplatted lands. 
 
403.3 Local Street Arrangement 
Arrange local streets to discourage their use by traffic originating outside 
the immediate neighborhood. 
 
403.4 Topography 
Arrange streets in relation to topography as to produce desirable lots of 
maximum utility and streets of reasonable gradient, safe ingress -egress 
and to facilitate adequate surface drainage. 
 
404 Transportation Planning Criteria 
 
404.1 Design Year 
The Design Year for future traffic volumes will be 20 years from the start 
of the design process. The Design Engineer will confirm the design year 
for a project before starting the design process.

404.2 Adjustments to Design Year ADT Volumes 
Adjustments may be required in anticipation of major land developments 
or significant changes to nearby roadways that will affect future traffic 
volumes expected on the roadway under design. Adjustments in traffic 
volumes for major land developments will follow the Traffi c Impact 
Procedures. Adjustments for other impacts shall be approved by the 
County before being undertaken by the Design Engineer. 
 
404.3 Design Hour Volume 
The Design Hour Volume (DHV) is the traffic volume used to determine 
the number of traffic lanes needed on the roadway. The DHV is from the 
Design Year, which requires County approval.  
 
The number of lanes for each direction of traffic for an interim roadway is 
determined by the traffic impact analysis. Design the interim roadway for 
conversion to the ultimate section determined by classification. 
 
For special activity centers such as recreational areas, factories, sports 
arenas, etc., other values of the above factors will be used. It is also 
recognized that special traffic conditions may or will exist that require 
modification of the above factors.  In these two sets of cases, document 
the different factors that are approved for use by the County. 
 
404.4 Turning Movements 
At major intersections and at driveways leading to major activity centers, 
the design hour turning volumes are important in determining the 
intersection capacity, resulting number of lanes, and the storage length 
for exclusive turning lanes required for ea ch approach. For intersections 
being reconstructed and that are in fully developed areas, existing turning 
movement percentages will be collected in the field and are assumed to 
be the same for the future design year. For new intersections or for those 
significantly impacted by new land developments or major changes to 
nearby roadways, existing and projected traffic data along with 
engineering judgment will be used to reassign vehicle trips on nearby 
street networks to derive the turning movements at project intersections. 
 
Analyze turning movements for both a.m. and p.m. peak hours at project 
intersections so that the maximum turning or through volumes can be 
determined for each approach. In the absence of other data, it can be 
assumed that the ‘background’ street network intersectio n turning

In certain areas of the County such as large retirement communities, the

404.5 Other Traffic Volume Reduction Factors 
Vehicle trip (traffic volume) reductions for future transit ridership or other 
transportation modes are not permitted. Reductions for "passer -by or' 
diverted' trips are allowed as per the Institute of Transportation Engineers 
(ITE) Trip Generation Manual ( latest revision) but must first be approved 
by the County. Trip reductions for special land uses utilizing travel demand 
management strategies will be considered on a case -by-case basis. 
However, the factors used must be fully and accurately documented to 
the County’s satisfaction. 
 
404.6 Capacity Analysis 
Use s oftware based on  the current Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 
procedures to determine the capacity and the resulting number of lanes 
for roadway design project street sections and intersections. For rural 
street sections with existing or planned traffic signals more than a m ile 
apart, use the appropriate section of the HCM. For urban or suburban 
areas where traffic signals are at or less than a mile apart, assume that 
the signalized intersection capacity will control the design of the roadway 
segments. 
 
The number of through lanes on street sections must be consistent with 
the number of through lanes at adjacent intersections. For capacity and 
lane determination, assume major intersections are to be signalized for 
the design year. Use the signalized intersection section of the HCM for 
the analysis. Use t he default values of the peak hour factor (PHF), 
percentage of trucks, and saturation flow rate. Other input criteria will be 
those equal to existing or future traffic conditions and approved by County.

404.7 Future Traffic Volumes 
Use f uture traffic volumes to ensure that the road has enough traffic -
carrying capacity. The general unit of measure for traffic on a road is the 
ADT, the total volume of traffic in a given time period divided by the 
number of days in that time period. Use engineering judgement to derive 
the future ADT of growth patterns in the area with concurrence from the 
County. 
 
The traffic volume during a period of time shorter than a day shall be used 
for design purposes, reflecting peak hour periods. For roads with unusual 
or highly seasonal fluctuation in traffic volumes, use the 30th-highest hour 
of the design year. 
 
The directional design hour volume is the traffic volume for the rush hour 
period in the peak direction of flow. Use directional distribution factors 
based on existing traffic counts. If this information is not available, assume 
that 60% of the traffic is going in one direction. For a more detailed 
analysis of intersection and road capacity, use the procedures as 
described in the intersection portion of this manual and the of the HCM. 
 
405 Traffic Impact Procedures 
One of Navajo County’s key objectives is to operate and maintain a safe 
and efficient roadway system. The review and management of 
development-generated traffic is an integral part of reaching this goal. The 
Traffic Impact Procedures as outlined in this do cument have been 
established to meet this objective. These Traffic Impact Procedures 
establish a range of traffic impact study categories based on the 
characteristics of the development and the estimated peak hour traffic 
volumes. The procedures also outli ne the analysis approach and 
methods. 
 
The purpose of this document is to provide criteria for the preparation of 
Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) or a Traffic Impact Statement (TIS) for new 
land developments or additions to existing developments and to establish 
the report format for these studies.

These procedures are intended to: 
• assist developers through the approval process by outlining the 
requirements and level of detail of traffic analysis that will be 
required of them during the approval process  
• standardize the types and details of analysis required in the 
assessment of traffic impacts for developments with similar levels 
of size and intensity  
• ensure consistency in the preparation and review of a TIA through 
standardization of the reports 
 
A TIA identifies existing traffic volumes and conditions, development traffic 
volumes, and conditions and their combined impacts on the existing and 
future roadway system. Additionally, a TIA analyzes traffic circulation both 
on- and off-site. This is a us eful tool for early identification of potential 
traffic problems and can play an important part in the success of a 
development. Assess the need for a TIA as early as possible in the 
development process when there is maximum flexibility to mitigate traffic-
related impacts. The results of the TIA can also affect the Site Plan or 
development proposal, so it is important to begin the traffic analysis early 
and incorporate the TIA recommendations into the development plans 
during design. 
 
The procedures are to assist developers through the approval process by 
outlining the requirements and level of detail of traffic analysis required of 
them during the approval process. Additionally, these procedures 
standardize the types and details of ana lysis required in the assessment 
of traffic impacts to ensure consistency in the preparation and review of a 
TIA.  
 
405.1 Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) Categories 
Most developments require a TIA prepared by a Registered Professional 
Engineer in the State of Arizona. The County Engineer may waive the 
requirement for a TI A for developments generating fewer than 100 peak 
hour trips. Estimate the peak hour trips utilizing the most recent edition of 
the Institute of Transportation Engineers’ (ITE) Trip Generation Manual or 
other relevant data as approved by the County Engineer. The developer 
should initially identify the land use, intensity, and estimated number of 
daily, AM, and PM peak hour vehicle trips generated by the proposed 
development to determine the level of analysis. The developer may 
schedule a  pre-TIA scoping meeting immediately following the pre -

The developer shall first estimate the number of vehicle trips generated 
by the development to determine the applicable TI A category and shall 
obtain concurrence from the County Engineer on the number of trips 
generated by the development. 
 
The specific analysis requirements and level of detail are summarized in 
Table 406.1 and are determined by the following categories. 
 
405.1.1 Category I 
Developments which generate 100 or more peak hour trips but fewer than 
500 trips during the morning or afternoon peak hour. A Category I TIA may 
be required for sites less than 100 trips during the highest peak hour for 
any of the following reasons: 
1. The existence of any current traffic problems or concerns in the 
local area such as an offset intersection, a high number of traffic 
accidents, etc. 
2. The sensitivity of the adjacent neighborhoods or other areas where 
the County Engineer may perceive an adverse impact based on 
public or other input. 
3. The proximity of proposed site driveways to existing driveways or 
intersections. 
4. Other specific problems or safety related concerns that may be 
aggravated by the proposed development. 
 
Should any of these conditions arise t he County Engineer will evaluate 
the need for a TIA based on the issues. 
 
405.1.2 Category II 
Developments which generate 500 or more peak hour trips but fewer than 
1000 trips during the highest peak hour. 
 
405.1.3 Category III 
Developments which generate 1000 or more peak hour trips but fewer 
than 1500 trips during the highest peak hour.

405.2 Traffic Impact Statement (TIS) 
A development or revisions to an existing develop site that generates less 
than 100 peak hour trips should submit a TIS. The TIS is a scaled down 
and simplified version of the TIA and is intended for very small projects 
that will have minimal impacts on existing traffic as compared to the larger 
type developments. It shall address pertinent features of the proposed 
development which may impact traffic on the existing roadways adjacent 
to the site.  
 
The TIS shall include but not be limited to: 
1. Description of Existing Conditions 
a. Roadways, including existing street cross -section, 
functional classification, posted speed limit, daily traffic 
volume, and the 85th percentile speed (if available). 
b. Intersections, including existing lane configuration and 
traffic control, including stop signs and signals. 
c. Nearby driveways (adjacent, opposite and off-set), including 
locations and spacing. 
d. Sight distance deficiencies. 
e. Surrounding Land Use. 
f. Transit, Pedestrian, and Bicycle facilities and access. 
2. Description of Proposed development 
a. Location. 
b. Vicinity map and/or site plan, including spacing of driveways 
and distance from nearest intersection and other driveways, 
including opposite and off-set.  
c.  Land Use & Project Size. Use the appropriate ITE Land Use 
code when feasible. Provide an opening year and/or 
buildout date if known.  
d. Hours of operation, if known 
e. Access, including location, type (full partial, right -in/right-
out), spacing and alignment with existing/future driveways

3. Trip Generation 
a. Daily, AM, and PM peak hour traffic. For developments with

Identify whether a significant number of peak hour trips will

any mitigation measures that will be taken to accommodate

4. Level of Service 
a. LOS for one or more movements at site access drives, if 
requested. Typically, this is requested to determine if left or 
right turns into or out of the project site will be required or 
allowed. 
5. Street Classification and Circulation Map.  
a. Discuss the functional classification and circulation map 
related to the County road system. 
6. Additional Site-Specific Analyses 
a. Additional site -specific analyses may be required at the 
request of the County Engineer. 
b. Discuss any other features of the project which could have 
an adverse impact on existing traffic. These could include 
seasonal or off-peak operations, etc.  
c. Include recommendations for roadway improvements 
needed due to site generated traffic.

406 TIA Analysis Approach and Methodology 
Prior to beginning any analysis, the developer , or his authorized 
representative, should schedule a Pre -TIA Scoping Meeting with  the 
County to discuss the  project scope and required/expected level of 
analysis to be performed by the engineer completing the TIA. Study 
intersections, time periods, horizon year(s), required traffic counts, 
intersections needing traffic signal warrant analysis, and future adjace nt 
developments will be identified. Larger developments may require 
additional discussion concerning Collector and Arterial streets. Applicants 
should contact the County to request a pre -TIA Scoping Meeting to 
determine the analysis requirements of the TIA.  
 
406.1 Project Description 
The TIA shall discuss the proposed project including type (residential, 
commercial), size (number of lots, building square footage) along with 
expected opening dates. The description should include the number of 
acres and a general description of the surro unding area (agricultural, 
suburban). This section should also include a discussion of jurisdictional 
boundaries. Which jurisdictions besides Navajo County may be affected 
by the project and which other jurisdictions may need to approve the traffic 
study or issue construction permits.

overall trip generation in accordance with the criteria in Table 406.1. The 
County Engineer may adjust the limits of the study area. 
 
Analyze the roadways and intersections within the study area with and 
without the proposed development to identify any projected impacts 
regarding level of service and safety. 
 
The a pplicant should reference the County’s  Capital Improvement 
Program (CIP) , Comprehensive  Plan, Area and Transportation Plans, 
Character Area Maps, and expected modal levels of service for the area 
and place type as they appear in the latest regional plan. Existing

406.3 Study Horizon Years 
The study horizon years will be determined by project type and size of 
development in accordance with the criteria in Table 406.1. Identify and 
discuss any known, approved, or planned significant developments within 
the study area and the specified horizon year. At a minimum, evaluate 
opening year. Evaluate buildout year when it is different from opening 
year. Unless otherwise specifi ed by the County, evaluate a minimum of 
five years after buildout.  
 
406.3.1 Project Phasing 
State whether the project will be one or multiple phases. Multiple phasing 
shall identify each phase and state the roadway improvements 
constructed with each phase to maintain an acceptable level of service 
(LOS). Phasing must relate to the horizon year. I nclude the number of 
trips generated and timeline for each phase if known. Indicate if traffic 
studies for large and multiple phased projects will be submitted for future 
phases. 
 
406.4 Analysis Time Period 
The TIA shall analyze the impact of traffic generated by the development 
for the typical traffic peak hours. Peak hours generally occur during both 
the morning and afternoon weekday peak hours, typically between 
7:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. respectively. Normal 
peak hours may vary under certain conditions as described below:  
1. If the proposed project is expected to generate no trips or a very 
low number of trips during either the morning or evening peak 
periods, the requirement to analyze one or both periods may be 
waived by County.  
2. Analyze peak hours where the peak traffic hour in the study area 
occurs during midday weekday (schools require an analysis of the 
peak period during the school start -up and school let -out), or 
occurs on a weekend (park events, shopping centers, church 
facilities), or if the proposed project has unusual peak hour 
characteristics (such as retirement areas). 
 
Conduct roadway segment analysis for average daily traffic (ADT) and 
peak hours. The County may require additional time periods if the 
development has unusual peaking characteristics such as a church, 
school, shift work, sports complex, movie theater, etc.  or if the adjacent

406.5 Seasonal Adjustments 
Adjust t raffic volumes for the analysis hours for the peak season if 
determined appropriate by the County. County approval is required for use 
of seasonal adjustment. The intent is not to assess maximum peak hourly 
volumes, such as the day after Christmas for a retail development, but to 
address peak seasonal volumes. For example, traffic counts collected in 
January, and the peak traffic period occurs during the summer months, 
then adjust the counts to summer months. 
 
Under the condition whereby the majority of the development’s trips are 
anticipated to travel to external locations (e.g., Phoenix, etc.) along State 
highways, the author should obtain seasonal adjustment factors from 
ADOT and determine the applicability of such factors to any collected daily 
traffic counts. 
 
406.6 Data Collection 
Collect a ll data in accordance with the latest edition of the Institute of 
Transportation Engineers Manual of Transportation Engineering Studies  
or as directed by the County if not specifically covered in the ITE manual. 
 
Include the following existing and proposed conditions within the study 
area. 
 
406.7 Existing Conditions 
 
406.7.1 Roadway Configuration 
Discuss roadway configuration and geometry, including roadway 
classification, lane and shoulder width, number of lanes, turning lanes, 
including elevation or grade differences. Discuss the location of nearby 
driveways, lane configuration at intersections a nd any striping 
configurations such as extra wide lanes, carrots, etc.

406.7.2 Traffic Volumes 
Discuss both existing ADT’s and turning movement counts in this section. 
Present the current and projected daily traffic volumes in the report. 
1. Obtain both AM and PM turning movement counts for all existing 
intersections directly adjacent to or within proximity where the 
proposed site traffic will have a direct impact on the intersection. 
The exact need for turning movement counts will depend on t he 
size and type of project and should be determined by the traffic 
engineer preparing the TIA as to what benefit they would be to the 
analysis. Extrapolate available turning movement counts a 
maximum of two years with concurrence of the County.  
2. Present the current and projected daily traffic volumes in the report. 
Obtain available daily count data from previous transportation and 
traffic studies and extrapolated a maximum of two years with the 
concurrence of the County Engineer. 
3. Traffic volume estimates from other approved developments within 
the study area which are expected to occur during the study 
horizon years should be obtained directly from those respective 
developments and included within the study report. 
4. Mechanical counts are required w here daily count data are not 
available, or such counts are over two-years old. 
 
406.7.3 Crash Data 
1. Obtain c rash data  for a 5 -year period  from the County Sheriff’s 
Office, Local Police Department s, ADOT or other source s as 
approved by the County. 
2. Obtain data for the most current 5-year period available. 
3. Present any collected records in the report. 
 
406.7.4 Traffic Control Devices 
1. Identify the location and type of traffic controls, including pavement 
markings, signs, and signals. 
2. Identify all traffic signals within the study area along with phasing, 
timing, and coordination programs. 
 
406.7.5 Existing Level of Service Analysis 
In this section, show and discuss the existing Level of Service (LOS) for 
all adjacent or nearby intersections. Identify and show both the AM and 
PM LOS for all existing turning movements. Further discuss any specific 
movement that has a LOS of E or F.

406.7.6 Other 
Obtain and include any current or planned County transportation

406.8 Project Conditions 
 
406.8.1 Trip Generation 
1. Use the latest edition of ITE’s Trip Generation Manual for selecting 
trip generation rates for the proposed development. Use the 
guidelines contained in the Trip Generation Manual  to determine 
whether the average trip generation rate or equation is appropriate. 
2. Refer to the land use categories in the ITE’s Trip Generation 
Manual and use the appropriate category for the proposed project. 
Refer to this traffic as site traffic. If the proposed project does fall 
into one of the ITE land use categories, then clearly explain which 
trip generation category is the most appropriate and why. 
3. Use other rates if ITE’s Trip Generation Manual  does not include 
rates for the specific land use, or the available data is limited, or 
where local trip rates (if available) differ from the ITE rates. Obtain 
the County Engineer’s approval before using other rates.  
4. Use trip reduction factors due to internal capture and/or pass -by 
trips. If an internal capture rate greater than 15% is proposed, then 
clearly indicate and refer to other studies of comparable projects to 
justify the higher rate. For some projects, such as large commercial 
retail projects, both internal capture rate and pass -by trip 
reductions may be appropriate. Any internal capture rate or pass 
by trip reduction used shall follow the ITE calculation mythology 
and be clearly shown in a trip generation type summary table. 
 
406.8.2 Traffic Volumes/Distribution/Site Access 
Show ADT and AM/PM peak hour volumes using figures/exhibits that 
clearly indicate the year and for which movement the volumes apply. 
Show all movements for all access/driveways that will access the site, 
existing and proposed. Trip distribution is the perc entage or number of 
trips entering and leaving the site from each direction. Indicate the percent 
of trips (both AM/PM) in each direction for all driveways. Document and 
reference assumptions and/or data sources used in deriving trip 
distribution and assignment.

406.8.3 Background (Non-Site) Traffic 
Background traffic is defined as the volume of traffic on the roadway 
network surrounding and adjacent to the proposed development, but 
unrelated to the proposed development. Clearly identify background 
traffic, both average daily ADT and peak hour volumes  for existing 
conditions, opening year, and the predefined horizon year(s). 
 
406.8.4 Site Traffic 
Site traffic is the traffic generated by the proposed development. Indicate 
site traffic for average daily ADT and peak hour volumes. Include the 
opening year, buildout year (if different), and the horizon year(s) for the 
proposed site traffic. Projects th at include multiple phases, discuss the 
future phase traffic or if appropriate also shown in an exhibit or figure. 
 
406.8.5 Total Traffic 
Total traffic is the combination of the background traffic and site traffic. 
Indicate and show total traffic by the average daily ADT, peak hour 
volumes, buildout, and horizon year(s) or future phases. 
 
406.9 Capacity Analysis 
Perform capacity analysis on each of the major street and site 
intersections/driveways (signalized and stop controlled) in the study area 
and for the proposed site. The County accepts Level of Service (LOS) 
analysis performed using software such as Synchro and Highway 
Capacity Software (HCS) and may accept other analysis if first approved 
by the County. 
1. Compute the level of service using the latest edition of the Highway 
Capacity Manual or the latest version of HCS software. Calculate 
the LOS for each study area intersection directly impacted by the 
proposed site. Evaluate all movements at those intersections for 
both the AM and PM peak hours. Evaluate the LOS at each 
proposed driveway fo r all movements in both AM and PM peak 
hour. 
2. Perform operational analyses for signal-controlled intersections for 
opening year, project buildout, and for time horizons up to 5 years 
after buildout. 
3. For urban roadways, and rural highways where signal -controlled 
intersections are at or less than 1 mile apart, the capacity of the 
roadway is generally dominated by the capacity of the adjacent

406.10 Traffic Signal Needs 
Conduct a traffic signal needs study per the ADOT Traffic Manual section 
on the Traffic Signal Needs Study  for all new proposed signals for the 
base year. If warrants are not met for the base year, they should be 
evaluated for each year in the five-year horizon. 
 
Identify steps taken to mitigate any adverse effects of the traffic generated 
by the development on the street network within the study area. This shall 
include, but not be limited to: 
1. Improvements to existing signalized and unsignalized 
intersections. 
2. Future signalization of unsignalized intersections. 
3. Maintenance of street capacity at site driveways. 
 
Install traffic signals only when they meet needs per the ADOT Traffic 
Manual and as determined by the County.

406.11.1 Signal-Controlled Intersections 
For signal-controlled intersections, find the number of vehicles arriving at 
the intersection: 
 
 
 
406.11.2 Non-Signal/Stop-Controlled Intersections 
For non -signal-controlled intersections, find the number of vehicles per 
average 2-minute period: (from AASHTO) 
 
 
 
All results should be rounded up to the nearest 25-foot interval. 
 
Vehicles / cycle (for random arrivals) = 2 x (vehicles / hour) / (cycles / hour) 
 
Storage Length = Vehicles / cycles x 25 feet 
 
Example: Find the storage length required for 150 vph turning left if the 
signal cycle is 90 seconds. 
 
Vehicles / cycle = 2 x (150 veh / hr)(1 cycle @ 90 sec) / (3600 sec / hr) = 
7.5 veh / cycle 
 
Storage length = 7.5 veh / cycle x 25 feet = 187.5 feet  USE 200 feet 
Vehicles / 2 min period = (vehicles / hour) / (30 periods / hour) 
 
Storage Length = Vehicles / 2 min period x 25 feet 
 
Example: Find the storage length required for 150 peak hour vehicles 
turning left at a non-signal controlled intersection. 
 
Vehicles/2 min period = (150 veh / 1 hr) / (30 periods/hr) = 5 vehicles 
 
Storage Length = 5 veh x 25 feet = 125 feet USE 125 feet

406.12 Special Considerations 
1. Provide proper intersection sight distance at all development 
driveways/access points. The County uses AASHTO for 
determining sight distances.  
2. Consider vehicle type in the traffic study. If a proposed project is 
industrial or heavy commercial with a high percentage of large 
trucks (WB-40 or larger), evaluate auxiliary lane storage and return 
radii. 
3. For highways and/or roadways where the vehicle speed is higher 
than the posted speed limit, use a speed of 5 MPH over the posted 
speed limit or the 85 -percentile speed, as directed by the County, 
should be to estimate the safe stopping and intersection sig ht 
distances for highways and roadways with posted speeds of 35 
MPH or greater. 
 
406.13 Improvement Analysis 
Analyze impacts from the proposed development to the level of service 
and safety of roadways and intersections within the study area.  Evaluate 
all proposed driveways for LOS for all movements both AM and PM. 
 
Where roadways, intersections, intersection approaches, or lane groups 
operate in the horizon year(s) at level of service C or better without the 
development, mitigate the traffic impact s of the development on the 
roadway in the horizon year to a minimum level of service C.  
 
Where roadways, intersections, intersection approaches, or lane groups 
will operate below level of service C and greater than level of service of F 
in the horizon year(s) without the development, mitigate the traffic impact 
of the development to provide the same level of service at the horizon 
year(s). 
  
If roadways, intersections, intersection approaches, or lane groups 
operate at a level of service of F without the development – mitigation is 
required to maintain the same degree of level of service F (i.e. same 
duration of delay and queue length) which w ould occur without the 
development. 
 
Evaluate need for auxiliary lanes. See Chapter 600 for right and left turn 
lanes criteria. Analyze all proposed development driveways. If the 
development is proposing a full access driveway onto an arterial, and no

projects. Discuss the findings for the following:  
• Overall and peak hour LOS at all proposed driveways (all 
movements) for opening year, buildout year and horizon year. 
Discuss any potential conflicts with surrounding accesses (existing 
or planned). 
• Right and left turn lanes required with all storage shown. Discuss 
any roadway widening (arterials) required to accommodate left turn 
movements.

500 Environmental Analysis, Clearance, and 
Mitigation 
 
501 Federally Funded Projects 
Federally funded projects may involve the Arizona Department of 
Transportation (ADOT) and be subject to ADOT’s Environmental Planning 
process. 
 
502 Federal, State and County Regulations 
 
502.1 Environmental Analysis and Mitigation 
The County requires projects to comply with all requirements of the 
National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), as well as all other Federal, 
State, and local regulations. The County requires compliance of all 
parties, both public and private. 
 
For private development, the Developer is to obtain any required 
environmental permits or clearances. 
 
502.2 Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) 
ADEQ regulates water quality and the quality of storm water discharges. 
All improvements whether Public Works or Planning & Development 
Services shall adhere to ADEQ regulations. 
 
All utility design falling under the auspices of ADEQ shall be designed per 
the latest ADEQ requirements and submitted to them for approval prior to 
the issuance of the County permit. 
 
502.3 Section 404 Permit / Section 401 Water Quality 
Certification 
All projects that will require construction activity within a “water of the 
United States” must be reviewed in accordance with Section 404 of the 
Clean Water Act. Waters of the United States include all rivers, washes, 
drainages, ponds, etc., whether they have permanent water or not. The 
primary concern regarding waters of the United States is that if any “fill 
material” will be placed or “dredging activity” will occur (permanent or 
temporary) in an area under jurisdiction of the U.S. Army Corps of 
Engineers, then a Section 404 permit will be needed prior to construction.

Two types of Section 404 permits are available to meet the criteria of the 
Clean Water Act: nationwide permits and individual permits. A series of 
nationwide permits are used for smaller projects and require less time and 
effort to obtain. These permits can generally be acquired in 2 to 6 months. 
Individual permits are required for all projects where none of the 
nationwide permits are applicable; individual permits typically require 9 to 
12 months to acquire.  
  
In conjunction with the Section 404 permit, Section 401 Water Quality 
Certification must be coordinated with the Arizona Department of 
Environmental Quality. This coordination addresses water pollution 
prevention relative to project construction activities. 
 
502.4 Storm Water Quality 
Projects disturbing 1 acre, or more are subject to the National Pollution 
Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) requirements for construction 
sites under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) general permit for 
Arizona. Owners, developers, engineers, and/or contractors are required 
to prepare all documents required by this regulation, including but not 
limited to Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP), Notice of Intent 
(NOI) and Notice of Termination (NOT). 
 
As prescribed by the Arizona Pollutant Discharge Elimination System 
(AZPDES) General Permit for Discharge from Construction Activities to 
the Waters of the U.S., any development project in the County which will 
disturb 1 contiguous acres or greater, shall complete a Notice of Intent 
(NOI). See AZPDES for details. 
 
Stormwater runoff from construction sites cannot include pollutants such 
as phosphorous and nitrogen, pesticides, petroleum derivatives, 
construction chemicals, solid wastes, and sediment that adversely affect 
water quality.  
 
502.5 Hazardous Materials Investigations 
As part of the environmental clearance process potentially hazardous 
materials and/or underground storage tanks in the project area should be 
identified. If the project has the potential to encounter contamination or 
would acquire new right-of-way at the suspect site(s), a regulatory records 
review and preparation of a Preliminary Initial Site Assessment (PISA) is 
required. The results shall be documented in the proper environmental

document (EID, EDR, CE, EA, or EIS) and shall include any necessary

If hazardous materials are identified, or the potential for hazardous 
materials is perceived, then surface and subsurface investigations may be 
needed to determine the extent of contamination. The need for further 
investigation and/or mitigation will be de termined through consultation 
between the County, the party performing the survey/investigation, and 
the developer.  
  
In compliance with the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA) (29 
U.S. Code 651), the developer will investigate whether asbestos -
containing materials are present in structures subject to removal or 
modification. Additionally, painted surfaces, includin g but not limited to 
bridge structures, railings, poles, and pavement markings will be tested 
for the presence of lead-based paint if the features are to be demolished 
or modified or if pavement markings are to be removed. If the testing 
results in positiv e readings, the appropriate mitigation measures for 
workplace and public safety will be incorporated. 
 
502.6 Biological Resources 
All projects with the potential to affect natural biological resources or 
projects that may encounter protected or endangered plant or animal 
species must be reviewed. The Arizona Game and Fish Department On -
Line Environmental Review Tool will be accessed to determine the 
potential presence of protected, candidate, or species of concern and their 
habitat. If protected species are likely to be present, then a Biological 
Evaluation to determine the likelihood of impacts will be needed and will 
recommend avoidance or mitigation measures. If impacts to Endangered 
Species Act species cannot be avoided, consultation with the U.S. Fish 
and Wildlife Service is required whether or not the project is federally 
funded or has a federal nexus.

502.7 Cultural Resources 
All projects with potential impacts to cultural resources are required  to 
conduct a Cultural Resources Study in accordance with Federal, Tribal, 
and State laws and regulations. Submit the Study to the County for review 
and evaluation of the project’s impact(s) on archeological and cultural 
resources. If archaeological or cul tural resources are present, then the 
State Historic Preservation Office will be consulted to assist in the review 
and determination of options to prevent and mitigate damage to these 
resources including: 
• Altering the design to avoid archaeological and cultural resources. 
• Protecting the resources by utilizing methods to obscure them from 
view. 
• Mitigating the cultural resource, this involves removal and thorough 
documentation of the items by a professional archeologist. The 
documentation of the resource may then be interpreted as part of 
the design.  
 
503 Other Requirements 
 
503.1 Forest Service 
All projects within Forest Service areas shall follow the Forest Service 
NEPA Procedures and Guidance. 
 
503.2 Bureau of Land Management 
All projects on BLM land shall follow the Bureau of Land Management 
NEPA Procedures. 
 
503.3 Arizona State Land Department 
All projects on Arizona State Land Department (ASLD) shall follow ASLD 
Applications & Permits , including Right of Way and Cultural Resources 
requirements.

600 General Information 
The purpose of this  Chapter is to provide standards and geometric 
requirements for the design and construction of transportation 
improvements within the County . Transportation facilities may include 
roadways, traffic signals, street signing, pavement markings, pedestrian 
facilities, bicycle paths, and other facilities. The minimum requirements 
described herein are primarily based on safety considerations; therefore, 
under most circumstances, standards that provide a greater degree of 
safety may be used. 
 
601 Design Standards 
The use of widely accepted industry standards typically reduces design 
and review timeframes. Reference documents are cited in this section and 
are also listed in Chapter 200 . Note that these documents are revised 
periodically; therefore, users should use the most recent version of the 
document specified. 
 
County minimum design standards are described in AASHTO’s A Policy 
on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets , commonly referred to as 
the Green Book. 
 
See the Navajo County Standard Details , 600 series, for typical road 
cross-sections. For roadways which may be annexed in the near future 
by a city or town, the County may require elements of the adjacent city's 
or town's standards to be incorporated into the design. 
 
602 New Roads Accessing a County Maintained 
Road 
A new access road is any vehicular travel way that serves two or more 
lots or parcels. New public and private roads accessing a County 
maintained road shall require an approved Right -of-Way permit prior to 
construction. 
 
See Chapter 1200 and Chapter 1300. 
 
Consider using exclusive right-turn or left-turn lanes at major intersections 
and at locations where safety is significantly improved by providing a 
deceleration lane for vehicles turning out of the major roadway through 
lanes to make left or right turning  movements onto a crossroad or 
driveway. Turn lane design shall be per ADOT’s Traffic Engineering

and markings for turn lanes are as described by ADOT or MUTCD in 
reference manuals or as modified in these Design Standards. 
 
603 Survey and Road Monuments 
Install permanent survey monuments in accordance with Chapter 300.  
 
604 Federal Functional Classification 
Federal Functional Classifications are defined in Chapter 400. 
 
605 Design Speed 
The design of roadway geometrics, such as horizontal and vertical curves, 
depends upon the design speed selected for the roadway. The choice of 
the design speed is primarily determined by the Federal Functional 
Classification. The design speed is the maxim um speed for the safe 
operation of a vehicle that can be maintained over a specific section of a 
street when conditions are favorable so that the design features of the 
street govern. 
 
Design speeds for the various classifications of streets may be found in 
Table 605.1. The use of design speeds other than those outlined in Table 
605.1 must be approved by the County through a Waiver Request; see 
Appendix A. 
 
Design speeds are typically 5 to 10 mph over the anticipated operating 
speed.

606 Design Vehicle 
The design vehicle is the largest vehicle likely to use the road with 
considerable frequency. 
 
Table 606.1 Design Vehicle 
 
All streets and roadway access aprons  shall accommodate emergency 
vehicles. 
 
607 Alignments 
Design of the alignment must consider safety, profile, access, and 
intersection location(s). The combined effect of vertical and horizontal 
alignments along a given section of roadway is an important factor to 
consider. Although there are no specific design values or specific criteria, 
the following considerations should be addressed: 
1. Crest vertical curves should not be coincident with or immediately 
precede sharp horizontal curves. 
2. Avoid sharp horizontal curvature near the low point of a sag vertical 
curve. 
3. Horizontal and vertical curvature should be as flat as possible at 
intersections where vehicles have to decelerate, stop or 
accelerate.

for Geometric Design of Very Low-Volume Local Roads. When designing

1. Coordinate the design of horizontal and vertical alignments to avoid

discouraged.

the same direction separated by short tangent sections). Minimum 
distances are shown in Table 607.2. 
8. Sharp horizontal curves must not begin near the top of pronounced 
crest vertical curves or near the low point of pronounced sag 
vertical curves.

607.1.2 Compound and Reverse Curves 
Avoid the use of compound circular curves.  
 
In special cases, where topography or right-of-way constraints require the 
use of compound curves, the radius of the flatter curve should not exceed 
1.5 times the radius of the sharper curve.  
 
Where topographic or Right-of-Way constraints require the use of reverse 
simple curves, a minimum tangent separation between the curves shall 
be at least 100-ft or equal to at least 2/3 the super-elevation runoff length, 
whichever is greatest. When using reverse curves, special attention must 
be given to the roadway’s drainage requirements. An angle point is 
acceptable for breaks in tangent horizontal alignments of less than 1 
degree.

a roadway to compensate for the centrifugal forces created by horizontal

Examples of design superelevation rates based on the design speed, the 
radius of curve, and the superelevation rate can be found in AASHTO’s 
Green Book. 
 
When superelevation is introduced to account for horizontal curvature and 
to provide a stable turning motion for vehicles traveling at or below the 
design speed, the rotation of the pavement section must be designed 
along a given axis. The location of this axis of rotation has impacts on the 
length required to transition from a normal crown section to a 
superelevated section. The location can also impact drainage patterns, 
driver perception of the transition area, and aesthetics. Within a given 
project, the axis of rotation should remain constant for all horizontal curves 
and for a given type of cross section. Regardless of the location of the 
axis of rotation, review changes in cross slope between the roadway and 
its intersecting driveway and cross streets to avoid "flat” areas. 
 
Maintaining normal crown through curves on low -speed roads may be 
acceptable if maintaining the guidelines outlined in the AASHTO Green 
Book.  
 
607.2.1 Superelevation Transitions 
Superelevation transitions refer to the lengths of highway that are used to 
bring a normal crown section up to the superelevation rate that is being 
designed. Transitions are also used to bring a superelevated section back 
to the normal crown section. There are two components that make up the 
total transition for a superelevated section: 
1. Tangent Runout 
a. Denotes the length of highway needed to bring a normal 
crown section to a section with an adverse crown removed 
(zero cross slope), or vice versa. 
2. Superelevation Runoff 
a. Denotes the length of highway needed to bring a section 
with the adverse crown removed (zero cross slope) up to a 
fully superelevated section, or vice versa. 
 
Guidelines for the minimum length of superelevation runoff and tangent 
runout for a variety of design speeds and superelevation rates are given 
in the AASHTO Green Book.
