607.3.2 Vertical Curves 
All sections of a street’s vertical alignment must meet passing and 
stopping sight distance requirements for the design speed established for 
the street, while providing effective street drainage. Vertical curves should 
be made to provide greater stopping sight distance and more pleasing 
aesthetics. However, a minimum length vertical curve may be required to 
reduce the amount of excavation in rolling or hilly terrain. Refer to the 
AASHTO Green Book for vertical curve requirements and equations and 
Table 605.1 for design speeds. 
 
When designing crest or sag vertical curves for new or improved 
roadways, consider the following factors: 
1. The formulas used to establish the length of a vertical curve for 
crest situations can be found in the AASHTO Green Book. 
2. The formulas used to establish the length of vertical curve for sag 
situations can be found in the AASHTO Green Book. 
3. Grade beaks are acceptable as an alternative for a vertical curve if 
they are less than 1% or as approved by the County Engineer. 
4. Minimum lengths of crest vertical curves as determined by stopping 
sight distance requirements generally are satisfactory from the 
standpoint of safety, comfort, and appearance.  
5. The sight distance value for designing sag vertical curves is taken 
as the minimum safe stopping sight distance. The design will 
approximate the condition of headlight distance on the pavement 
at nighttime by using the stopping sight distance. The assumpti on 
for the design of sag vertical curves is that no continuous street 
lighting will exist, and that headlight distance will govern. 
6. The length of a vertical curve shall not be less than 200-ft or three 
(3) times the project design speed, whichever is greater. Most 
project designs should use a longer than minimum vertical curve 
length. Specific values for vertical curves, both tabular a nd 
graphical, can be found in the latest edition of the AASHTO Green 
Book. 
7. A smooth grade line with longer tangent grades and fewer vertical 
curves should be a design objective. 
8. Broken-back grade lines (two vertical curves in the same direction 
separated by short sections of tangent grade) should be avoided. 
9. For long upgrades, it is preferable to place the steepest grade at 
the bottom and reduce the grades at the top. Roller coaster and 
hidden dip profiles should be avoided.

607.3.3 Combined Horizontal and Vertical Curves 
The combined effect of vertical and horizontal alignments along a given 
section of roadway is important to consider. Although there are no specific 
design values or specific criteria, address the following items:  
1. Crest vertical curves should not be coincident with or immediately 
precede sharp horizontal curves.  
2. Sharp horizontal curvature near the low point of a sag vertical curve 
should be avoided.  
3. Horizontal and vertical curvature should be as flat as possible at 
intersections where vehicles have to decelerate, stop, or 
accelerate.

608.1 Stopping Sight Distance 
The principal design control for both crest and sag vertical curves is the 
provision of adequate stopping sight distance (SSD) along the entire 
length of the curve. All portions of the profile grade line shall meet sight 
distance requirements for the design speed of the roadway. 
 
Refer to the AASHTO Green Book for stopping sight distance information, 
specifically about the effects of grade on the stopping sight distance. 
 
Provide stopping sight distance throughout all parts of intersections. 
 
608.2 Passing Sight Distance 
On two-lane roadways, provision of passing sight distance (PSD) can be 
an important consideration. For crest vertical curves, the passing sight 
distance is substantially longer than the stopping sight distance, and the 
former is used as the design control.  Appropriate no-passing zones and 
markings must be in place to enforce the no passing criterion. For 
multilane roadways, the stopping sight distance is again used as the 
design control for vertical alignment. Refer to the AASHTO Green Book 
for a discussion of passing sight distances for various design speeds. 
 
608.3 Intersection Sight Distance 
Intersection sight distance (ISD) identifies areas at the corners of 
intersections of roads, driveways, and turnouts where views of 
approaching traffic should not be obstructed. Identify and show 
intersection sight distance triangles at all road intersecti ons, on the final 
subdivision plat, and on commercial site plans. Note these areas as 
“minimum clear sight triangle” and are required to remain free of all 
obstructions that would interfere with a driver’s visibility. The clear sight 
triangle is defined as anything between the heights of 3 ft and 10 ft, which 
often include buildings, signs, mailboxes, parked vehicles, walls/fences, 
vegetation etc. Exceptions (such as utility poles) may only be approved 
by the County Engineer. See ADOT’s Roadway Design Guidelines  and 
the AASHTO Green Book for additional information. 
 
608.4 Decision Sight Distance 
Decision sight distances given in AASHTO Table 3-3 should be provided 
when practical at intersections where a county road turns or intersects a 
State Route or as required by the County or designee. For measuring 
decision sight distance, use a 3.5-foot eye height and 2-foot object height,

609 Roadway Sections 
See the Navajo County Standard Details for typical sections. 
 
609.1 Cross Slope 
Surfaces of undivided streets shall have a normal crown that has a two -
way cross slope with the cross-section high point on the street centerline. 
The normal cross -slope is 2% on a paved road. A Waiver Request is 
required for a normal cross-slope greater than 2% and not exceeding 3% 
based on the following criteria: 
1. Road is not superelevated. 
2. Road is unpaved. 
3. Required for drainage needs, such as spread and dry lane criteria. 
4. Matching into an existing or restrictive condition. 
 
Review and evaluate roadway drainage as detailed in Chapter 800. 
 
Inverted crown streets will not be acceptable without approval of a Waiver 
Request. 
 
Any deviation from the desirable cross slope is subject to approval by the 
County Engineer through a Waiver Request. 
 
609.2 Traffic Lanes 
Table 609.1 shows appropriate ranges of road , bike, parking, turn, left - 
and right -turn lane and shoulder  widths. If severe constraints make 
preferred widths too costly, then use the “minimum” values as an absolute 
minimum. The Design Engineer must get prior approval from the County 
before using the “minimum” values. The Design Engineer shall prepare a 
design memo detailing the cross section and lane widths. All dimensions 
are in feet and measured to the center of lane lines.

609.2.1 Turn Lanes 
At intersections where no specific left-turn lane or a single left-turn lane is 
to be provided, the receiving lane on the exit portion of the intersection 
must have a minimum 18 -foot width measured from the outside edge of 
pavement to the edge of the left -turn lane, centerline, or to the edge of 
pavement of the center median if one is provided. 
 
At intersections where double left -turn lanes are to be provided, the 
receiving lanes on the exit portion of the intersection must have a 
minimum 30-foot width measured from the outside flow line to the edge of 
the left-turn lane, centerline, or the flow l ine of the center median, of one 
is provided. 
 
The length of the transition to match the standard cross section must be 
determined using the road width transition tapers as specified in 
Section 610. 
 
609.3 Shoulders 
The shoulder width is the minimum continuous width of shoulder providing 
a drivable paved, unpaved or a combination thereof surface. The drivable 
width includes the usable portion of curb and gutter sections.  Shoulders 
shall be on each side of pavement.

609.3.1 Paved Shoulder 
Paved shoulder widths shall be per the Navajo County Standard Details, 
500 Series.  The shoulder slope shall match the cross -slope of the 
adjoining travel lane unless site specific conditions prevent it. 
 
609.3.2 Unpaved Shoulder 
Unpaved shoulder widths shall be a minimum of 4 feet wide. Unpaved 
shoulder slopes shall be 20:1 (5%) max unless site specific conditions 
prevent it. 
 
609.4 Side Slopes 
The stability of all cut and fill slopes steeper than 2:1 shall be determined 
by a geotechnical study submitted by a registered engineer with 
proficiency in Geotechnical Engineering and approved by the County 
Engineer.  
 
Typical cut and fill slopes shall be per the ADOT Construction Standard 
Drawings, C-02.10 to C-02.30.  
 
Cut/fill slopes steeper than 2:1 and in excess of six (6) feet shall be slope 
stabilized and an erosion control plan shall be submitted for review and 
approval to the County Engineer or designee.  
 
Refer to the AASHTO Roadside Design Guide for non-typical cases. 
 
610 Pavement and Lane Transitions 
Pavement transitions should be consistent with the section having the 
higher design standards. Place transitions on a tangent alignment section 
without horizontal and vertical sight distance restrictions. Desirably, the 
entire transition is visible to the driver approaching the narrower section. 
Avoid intersections within the transition. Drivers approaching the transition 
need to recognize and evaluate the situation and then decide on their 
course of action. The sight distance provided at pavement transitio ns 
should be significantly greater than the minimum stopping sight distance. 
Sight distances in the order of 1.5 to 2.0 times the minimum stopping sight 
distances would be appropriate for transitions on rural highways and 
urban controlled-access highways respectively.

611.1 Barriers 
The installation of roadside barriers is required per the AASHTO Roadside 
Design Guide . Install r oadside barriers in accordance with the current 
ADOT Standard Specifications, Construction Standard Drawings and 
Approved Products List. 
 
Provide barriers, concrete or guardrail, when necessary for the safety of 
the traveling public, as well as protection for adjacent properties. The 
need for barrier should be determined at the early stages of design to 
ensure that road sections are designed with enough width to facilitate the 
barrier installation. Guardrail requires additional coordination to ensure 
that drainage pipes have sufficient cover for the installation of posts and 
are extended to accommodate the necessary adjustments in the 
embankments and slopes. 
 
The following minimum guidelines for barrier installation are based on the 
AASHTO Roadside Design Guide. However, it is noted that guardrail may 
be required in some locations that do not necessarily meet these criteria 
based on the judgment of the County. Such factors as traffic volumes, 
speed of traffic, accident history, road curvature, slopes of recovery area, 
presence of curb and gutter, and location of trees, utility poles, etc. must 
all be considered when determining if guardrail is warranted in a spe cific 
location. 
 
Barriers are typically required on sections of roadway when any of the 
following conditions exist within the clear zone, as defined in the AASHTO 
Roadside Design Guide: 
1. A roadside parallel embankment (fill slope) of 3:1 or steeper and a 
depth of 4 ft or more 
2. A water hazard with a depth of 2 ft or more 
3. A ditch section with a depth of 3 ft or more 
4. A fixed object (such as a culvert, pipe, headwall, retaining wall, 
bridge pier, or abutment) 
5. Other hazards as determined by the County 
 
The County shall make the final determination as to whether a barrier is 
warranted along a section of roadway based on a review of the plans, a

field inspection after rough grading has been completed, and/or prior to 
final acceptance. 
 
New roadside barriers shall be MASH compliant and approved for use by 
FHWA and ADOT. 
 
611.2 Longitudinal Rumble Strips 
Longitudinal rumble strips may be required where deemed necessary by 
the County. Longitudinal rumble strips should be applied to new 
construction centerline and shoulders when the thickness of the asphaltic 
concrete will allow placement in accordance with ADOT’s Traffic 
Engineering Group Traffic Guidelines and Processes (T GP) 480  titled 
"Longitudinal Rumble Strips".  
  
Placement criteria is shown in ADOT’s TGP 480. Details of rumble strip 
applications are in ADOT’s Signing and Marking Standard Drawings and 
must be shown on traffic plans.  
  
In general, rumble strips are applied on the centerline and shoulders of 
rural roadway sections and should not be applied in urban, developed, or 
developing areas. In suburban areas, a determination will be made for 
each project through coordination with t he County on whether rumble 
strips are appropriate.  
  
Rumble strips may be applied on existing roadway sections to reduce the 
potential for run-off-road and crossover crashes. 
 
611.3 Safety Rails 
Install safety rails for the protection of pedestrians when slopes are 2:1 or 
steeper, within 3 feet of a sidewalk or other walkway, and the embankment 
height of the slope exceeds 3 feet, unless otherwise approved by the 
County Engineer or designee. Safety  rails may also be required as 
directed by the County. Installation of safety rail does not remove the 
Engineer’s responsibility for designing per AASHTO’s Roadside Design 
Guide. 
 
Install safety rails in accordance with MAG Detail No. 145. Variations may 
be approved by the County Engineer or designee through a Waiver 
Request.

612 Roadway Surface 
The paving of roads and streets shall be based on FFC and context. The 
type of pavement surface shall be determined by the following criteria: 
1. All roads shall be paved, except in subdivisions in which the 
minimum parcel size is greater than five (5) acres. Minimum paved 
structural sections can be found in Table 612.2 
2. A penetration double chip seal over adequate base material may 
be utilized on new residential subdivision streets with lot sizes 
greater than two (2) acres or more when grades, snow removal, 
and/or traffic volumes are compatible, and the streets will be 
privately maintained. The maximum grade allowed for a 
penetration double chip seal is 10%. Grades exceeding 10% shall 
have an asphaltic concrete surface. The County will not accept any 
roads into their maintenance system that are double chip sealed. 
 
Special consideration may be given when specifying a road surface type, 
based upon consideration of the following or a combination of the 
following:  
1. Total development build-out  
2. Traffic volumes or traffic analysis  
3. Geometries  
4. Snow removal  
5. Location  
6. Grades 
7. Subgrade conditions 
 
612.1 Subgrade 
Subgrade shall be prepared in accordance with MAG Specifications 
Section 301. The materials of the subgrade shall conform to and be 
constructed in accordance with MAG Specifications Section 702.

612.2 Select Material 
Select material shall conform to MAG Specification Section 702 for 
processed natural materials and decomposed granite. 
 
612.3 Aggregate Base Course (ABC) 
Aggregate base course materials and construction shall conform to ADOT 
Specifications Section 303, unless otherwise approved by the County 
Engineer or designee. Use Class 2 aggregate base under roads, 
sidewalks, and driveways; however, other classes may be  considered 
based on site and soil conditions. 
 
612.4 Asphalt Pavement Design 
The structural design for the placement of asphaltic concrete and base 
material, shall be based upon the Asphalt Institute methods, AASHTO 
Guide, ADOT Pavement Design Manual, or other methods as approved 
by the County Engineer or designee. 
 
County roads shall have a pavement structural section based on the 
average daily traffic (ADT), FFC, equivalent 18 -kip single -axle loads 
(ESALs), and R-Value of subgrade soils and/or sub-base materials under 
the roadway. The pavement structural section shall not be less than the 
values shown in Table 612.2. 
 
A Pavement Design Report prepared and sealed by a professional 
engineer registered in the State of Arizona and approved by the County 
Engineer or designee is required to determine the pavement structural 
section(s). The evaluation should be based on good engineering 
judgment utilizing the best information available during the planning and 
design phases of the project together with consideration of the following 
project specific conditions: 
• Pavement Design Life 
• Traffic Considerations (ADTs, ESALs, etc.) 
• Subgrade Soil Conditions 
• Weather 
• Availability of Materials 
• Constructability 
• Maintainability 
• Cost Comparisons (initial capital cost and life cycle)

614 Intersections 
The goal of the design in providing intersection layouts is to allow for safe 
and efficient crossing, merging, and diverging of conflicting vehicle 
streams. These conflicts can be significantly reduced through the 
provision of adequate sight distances and efficient traffic control devices. 
Providing safe sight distances and effective control will depend on human 
factors related to the drivers, bicyclists, and pedestrians, the traffic 
volumes to be accommodated, and the geometric and topographical 
characteristics of the intersection itself.  
 
The crossover crown of a roadway being intersected shall not exceed an 
algebraic difference of 4 percent for arterial and collector roads and 8 
percent for local roads. 
 
Intersections should be located along tangent sections of roadway. In no 
case shall an intersection be located on or near the inside of a sharp 
curve. 
 
Refer to AASHTO’s guidelines for design of intersections  and the ADOT 
Roadway Design Guidelines for information about roundabout design. 
 
614.1 Location and Configuration 
Intersections shall be created or revised per the following guidelines: 
1. Intersections shall be located per Chapter 1300. 
2. 90-degree intersections are preferable to skewed intersections 
3. Skews greater than three degrees on arterial and collector roads 
and skews greater than five degrees on residential and local roads 
are to be avoided and require approval of the Navajo County 
Engineer.

614.3 Cul-de-Sacs 
A cul-de-sac is a street termination that serves more than one (1) and less 
than twenty (20) property owner(s) and has only one direct access to the 
public street system. The length of a cul-de-sac is measured between the 
centerline of an intersecting street and the radius point of the cul-de-sac.  
 
See Table 614.2 for cul-de-sac design criteria including minimum radii and 
maximum lengths. 
 
Table 614.2 Cul-de-Sac Design Requirements 
 
A Design Waiver  may be made where topography or geographical 
constraints exclude meeting all cul-de-sac criteria.

408.12. 
 
614.5 Deceleration Lanes, Left -Turn and Right -Turn 
Channelization 
Deceleration lanes and additional right -of-way may be required  on 
collectors and arterials as required by the County and TIA. Factors to be 
taken into consideration when performing a warrant study such as 
shoulder width, percentage of trucks, sight distance, roadway grade, 
horizontal and vertical curvature, and crash history. The lane length must 
be determined on a case -by-case basis and must be approved by the 
County Engineer or designee.

A left-turn lane serves to expedite the flow of through traffic, to control the 
movement of turning traffic, and to improve the safety and capacity of the 
intersection. 
 
Justify right -turn lanes based on capacity improvements and safety by 
permitting vehicles to slow down, stop as required and then turn right 
without impeding the flow of through traffic. Right turns are usually made 
at lower speeds than through movements, safety is enhanced if the slower 
turn is made in a separate, exclusive lane. 
 
See ADOT’s Roadway Design Guidelines , Chapter 400, for additional 
information. 
 
614.6 Turn-Lane Warrants 
For left- and right-turn lane warrants, see ADOT’s TGP Section 245 "Turn 
Lane Warrants". 
 
614.7 Traffic Islands and Raised Medians 
See ADOT’s Roadway Design Guidelines , Chapter 400, Subsection 
408.13 for additional information on traffic islands and raised medians. 
 
Raised medians may be placed at subdivision entrances or can be used 
to create a divided roadway. All medians greater than 6 feet in width shall 
be landscaped in accordance with Chapter 1000 . A  maintenance 
agreement from a homeowners’ association (HOA) or other group  is 
required. Construct medians 6-foot or less with concrete, per ADOT 
Construction Standard Drawing No. C -05.40; see Chapter 1000  for 
additional information. Deviations from these criteria requires approval 
from the County Engineer or designee. 
 
Construct median nose transitions in accordance with ADOT Construction 
Standard Drawing No. C-05.40.

On roadways without curb and gutter, roadside drainage ditches or 
channels shall be in accordance with the drainage analysis and the 
drainage plan as approved by the County. Capture and convey drainage 
on streets with curb and gutter via a storm drain system.

616 Bicycle and Pedestrian Facilities 
All design and construction shall attempt to meet and conform to the 
current standards, where practical. Pedestrian facilities, including shared 
use paths, within the public right-of-way shall use the U.S. Access Board 
Accessibility Guidelines for Pedestrian Facilities in the Public Right -of-
Way (PROWAG) . PROWAG is published under the ADA to address 
access to sidewalks and streets, crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian 
signals, on-street parking, and other features within public right-of-way. 
 
616.1 Bicycles 
It is the County’s goal to develop a transportation infrastructure that 
provides safe and convenient bicycle access. The County further 
advocates that bicyclists have the right to operate in a legal manner on all 
County roads including fully controlled -access highways except where 
specifically excluded by administrative regulation and where posted signs 
give notice of a prohibition. The County may consider the installation of 
dedicated bicycle lanes when the incremental costs for construction and 
maintenance are funded by a property owner or HOA and the bicycle lane. 
 
Use the AASHTO Guide for the Development of Bicycle Facilities  for 
bicycle facilities in the County.

616.5 Accessibility 
The U.S. Access Board publishes guidelines for pedestrian facilities 
located within public right-of-way that are issued under the Americans with 
Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Architectural Barriers Act (ABA).  
 
Design all new or updated features in Couty right-of-way shall comply with 
the US Access Board’s Pedestrian Facilities in the Public Right -of-Way 
(PROWAG).  
 
All new or updated features outside of County right-of-way shall adhere to 
ADA and ABA guidelines. 
 
617 Driveways 
A Right-of-Way permit is required prior to constructi ng a driveway. Site 
plans submitted to the County for review shall include dimensions, radii, 
and grades for all proposed driveways. See Chapter 1300 for additional 
information and requirements. Paved turnouts are classified as driveways.  
 
The number, location, or spacing of driveways may be limited for arterial 
street classifications to ensure their primary function of mobility. 
Conversely, the primary function of local streets is to provide access, and 
therefore driveway spacing is less restrictive. 
 
When a development is located adjacent to a public street, the parking 
facility must accommodate full internal vehicular circulation and storage. 
Vehicular circulation must be located completely within the property and 
vehicles within one portion of the de velopment must have access to all 
other portions of the same development without using the adjacent street 
system.

sections. 
 
617.1 Fire and Emergency Services Access 
All site/civil and building plans shall meet the submittal requirements of 
the County and the Fire Department. The driveway and fire lane 
dimensions, percent grades, turning radii and design specifications, 
including load capacity, shall be clearly identif ied on the plans. The 
following criteria shall apply to the design of driveways and fire lanes: 
• 13’-6” minimum vertical clearance; 
• Existing and proposed traffic patterns of driveways, and/or 
proposed fire lanes identifying and labeling all physical barriers to 
vehicular access including, but not limited to, gates, bollards, 
landscaping and similar items. The driveway and fire lane mus t 
provide access to all aspects of the building within 150 feet of the 
fire lane; 
• Fire lanes shall have a minimum unobstructed width of 20 feet for 
one way traffic, and 26 feet for two -way traffic with 25 feet inside 
turning radii and 50 feet outside turning radii; 
• Dead-end fire lanes shall be a maximum length of 150 feet;  
• No grade breaks greater than seven percent (7%); and, 
• Driveways and fire lanes shall have all-weather surface during and 
after construction. 
 
Emergency access drives shall be at least 24 feet in width. 
 
These are the primary design criteria for driveway design. The County 
and/or Fire Department reserve the right to modify or add design criteria 
as necessary to enforce the applicable life and fire safety codes during 
plan review or construction inspection.

617.2 Number of Driveways  
The number of driveways is a function of the size and use of the property. 
If additional driveways are requested, they shall adhere to the minimum 
spacing requirements noted herein . Where a property has access to 
multiple roads, the County reserves the right to restrict access to the road 
with the least amount of traffic.  
 
617.2.1 Additional Driveways 
Additional driveways may be permitted under the following conditions:  
• If the daily volume using one driveway exceeds 250 vehicles (in 
both directions).  
• If the traffic using one driveway exceeds the capacity of a stop -
sign-controlled intersection during peak street traffic hours or the 
peak site traffic hours.  
• If a traffic analysis shows that the traffic conditions warrant two or 
more driveways. 
 
617.2.2 Driveway Spacing 
The County has established these guidelines for the minimum spacing 
between adjacent driveways, which vary depending on the land use and 
street type. Distances are measured from the centerline of the driveway. 
It is important to consider the location and s pacing of driveways as they 
have a direct impact on the safety and capacity of the roadway. 
 
To ensure safe and efficient traffic flow, the distance between adjacent 
driveways should be sufficient to allow vehicles entering or exiting the 
driveway to queue, accelerate, decelerate, and cross traffic without 
causing excessive interference with through traffic or other vehicles using 
the adjacent driveway. Whenever possible, driveways should align 
directly across from established driveways on the opposite side of the 
roadway. 
 
Driveways located near median openings shall either be centered with the 
center of the median opening or be at least 100 feet away from the median 
opening.

617.2.3 Joint Access  
A joint access is required for two adjacent developments when a proposed 
access does not meet these spacing requirements. Driveways shall not 
block access to streets, roads, properties, sidewalks, or other driveways. 
The spacing between adjacent driveways must be sufficient to allow 
vehicles to safely queue, accelerate, decelerate, and cross lanes without 
causing excessive interference with through traffic or other driveways. 
Private roads that provide access to two or more residential parcels shall 
provide a turnout in lieu of a single-use driveway. 
 
The developer must obtain, in writing, acknowledgement and approval 
from the area fire service providers regarding the proposed joint access 
driveway. 
 
If the developer does not use a restrictive covenant to require 
homeowners to park all vehicles off the joint access driveway surface, 
then the joint access driveway surface must be at least 24 feet wide. 
Otherwise, the driveway surface may be no less than 20 feet wide. 
 
The developer must install signs, approved by the County, indicating 
"private driveway" at the driveway entrance and include a plat note 
stipulating that maintenance of the driveway will not be the responsibility 
of the County. 
 
617.2.4 Driveway Analysis 
A Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) may be required to address traffic impacts 
for large developments , including multi -family, commercial or industrial . 
The County may require the developer to consolidate traffic access to a 
single point, which may be signalized or a roundabout. Driveway signals 
must be strategically placed to provide satisfactory signal progression for 
through traffic on the road.  
 
617.3 Driveway Design Criteria 
Driveways constructed within public right -of-way shall conform to the 
following criteria: 
1. If a curb inlet is present, the driveway shall be located such that the 
gutter depression is maintained, and 10 feet of separation remains 
between the inlet opening and the driveway. 
2. On all streets residential driveways are not appropriate, head -
in/back-out parking is generally prohibited. Such a condition

3. All driveways must be constructed within the street frontage of the 
subject property, as determined by extending the side property 
lines perpendicular to the curb line. Neither the driveway nor the 
curb returns shall overlap adjacent property frontage.  
 
Driveways may not exceed 70 percent of roadway frontage. 
 
617.3.1 Driveway Layout & Type 
Driveways can be constructed with different features such as curb and 
gutter, flared edges, paved turnouts, or radius returns. They can also be 
attached to the curb and gutter and made of various materials including 
concrete, Aggregate Base Course (ABC), and Asphaltic Concrete (AC). 
 
Figure 617.1 Driveway Types 
 
617.3.2 Driveway Restrictions 
New or modified driveways are not permitted  in the following conditions 
unless approved by the County:  
• Within 25 feet of the end of a guardrail 
• Within 100 feet of a bridge or other drainage structure 
• Within the minimum spacing described in this Manual 
• Within 150 feet of the right -of-way line of an intersecting arterial 
street 
• Within 100 feet of an approved median opening location  
• Within 25  feet from end arc of a curve connecting intersecting 
streets, as well as within the arc of the curve 
• When there is inadequate sight distance for vehicles on the 
driveway trying to access the street, those movements shall be 
prohibited

• For parking or loading areas that require backing maneuvers in

If a property cannot be served by an access point meeting these 
standards, the County may designate one or more access point(s) based 
on traffic safety, operational needs, and compliance with as many of the 
requirements as possible. A Waiver Request may be  submitted per 
requirements in Chapter 100. 
 
617.3.3 Width 
The design of a driveway should consider the space necessary to 
accommodate all vehicles using the driveway (adequate storage length). 
This applies to both vehicles making a left turn from the roadway and to 
vehicles stopped on the driveway waiting to ente r the roadway. The 
potential for larger vehicles, such as recreational vehicles (RVs) or 
livestock trailers, should be considered in the driveway design. 
 
617.3.4 Skew 
Driveway design shall seek to make the driveway alignment at a 90 -
degree angle (perpendicular) to the road they are accessing. When parcel 
circumstances cannot accommodate 90 degrees, a reduction of less than 
90 degrees, to a minimum of 60 degrees, may be considered for approval 
by the County. 
 
617.3.5 Driveway Length 
The lengths shown in Table 617.4 and Table 617.5 may be reduced, if 
approved by the County, after considering the following: 
1. Physical constraints on the site, such as existing structures; 
2. The impact upon on-site circulation; 
3. Shallow lot depths or unusual lot configurations; 
4. Existing or potential traffic movements which are unsafe or which 
have an adverse effect on traffic operations;

The driveway length is measure from the edge of road to the right-of-way 
or property line or to the first conflict within the parking lot on the site. 
 
617.3.6 Driveway Horizontal Alignment 
All multifamily, commercial, and industrial driveways on arterial streets 
shall be designed to align with opposing street or driveway or be offset by 
a minimum of 250 feet. 
 
All multifamily, commercial, and industrial driveways on collector streets 
shall be designed to align with opposing street or driveway or be offset by 
a minimum of 200 feet. 
 
617.3.7 Driveway Profile 
The vertical profile of a driveway shall be designed to provide a smooth 
transition to and from the roadway. Sufficient clearance between the 
vehicle and the driveway surface must be provided to prevent high 
centering and hang -ups; see ADOT Detail C-05.20 and C-06.10. The 
maximum grade for driveways should be limited to 10 percent for 
residential driveways and 7 percent for commercial driveways. 
 
The profile of driveway connections to uncurbed roadways shall match 
the roadway pavement and shoulder grades; an independent driveway 
profile may begin at the outer edge of the roadway shoulder.  
 
Successive crest grade breaks and successive sag grade breaks are to 
be spaced no closer than the spacing between the front and rear axles. 
For design of driveway profiles 20 feet is the minimum distance to be used 
between successive crest grade breaks or successive sag grade breaks 
unless the sum of the grade breaks is less than the maximum design 
grade change. For single family residential driveways used only by

Commercial/industrial driveways shall provide a minimum 20 -foot-long

617.3.8 Pedestrian Requirements 
When a driveway crosses or adjoins a sidewalk, walkway, or an 
accessible path, as defined by the US Access Board, the driveway grade 
shall not exceed 2 percent, over a minimum length of 3 feet, thereby 
effectively matching the cross slope of the sidewalk or accessible path of 
travel across the full width of the driveway. 
 
The local Fire Department shall be consulted when a grade change of 
greater than 7 percent is proposed. 
 
617.3.9 Channelized Driveways 
Channelized islands for limits driveway movements may be utilized, 
provided that the applicant establishes a maintenance agreement with the 
County. Where a sidewalk, walkway, or an accessible route, as defined 
by the US Access Board, crosses a limited move ment driveway island, 
the sidewalk shall be a minimum of 4 feet wide across the island and shall 
provide a continuous, uninterrupted detectable warning at the boundaries 
between the sidewalks and the driveways. 
 
Acceleration and deceleration lanes may be required to be incorporated 
into the design. Islands may be required with vertical curb. 
 
Additional right -of-way or easement may be required to accommodate 
these designs.  
 
The ends of the islands shall use a 2 -foot minimum radius at the face of 
curb. Where site plans do not permit installation of islands, the County 
may permit or require the installation of a center median on the adjacent 
public street as an alternative.

617.3.10 Driveway Sight Distance  
Adequate sight distance shall be provided for vehicles exiting and entering 
a driveway. Driveway locations shall be evaluated to determine whether 
a sight obstruction exists, such as buildings, fences, signs, vegetation, 
parked vehicles, horizontal or vertical highway alignments, etc.  Refer to 
AASHTO’s A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Street , for 
detailed information regarding sight distance at intersections. 
 
617.3.11 Drop-off and Turnaround Driveways 
When a site plan proposes the use of a drop -off or turn around type 
driveway for a commercial use such as drive -through bank, car wash, or 
school drop -off, the designer shall consider the vehicle queuing length 
and storage requirements so that the queue do es not extend back onto 
the street impeding free flow of traffic. Depending on the nature of the 
project, the County may require a TIA or queuing analysis to ensure the 
site plan design provides adequate storage and internal circulation to 
mitigate traffic impacts.

617.3.12 Drainage 
Driveways and turnouts shall be designed to adequately handle roadside 
drainage. Stormwater from the new roadway should not result in 
stormwater overtopping any part of the existing County-maintained travel 
way or cause erosion or deposition within the County Right- of-Way. New 
roadway, driveway or turnout shall be designed in such a way as to ensure 
that there is no increase in stormwater drainage onto neighboring 
properties. 
 
Drainage structures shall be provided under driveways when necessary. 
Flows (design storm events per Chapter 700) that can be accommodated 
with less than the minimum 18 -in. culvert size may use a concrete or 
paved low -flow drainage crossing. The Design Engineer shall provide 
details of the ditch or channel design and the embankment slopes with 
any protection requirements, including rip rap gradation. 
 
The County maintains a program related to the installation of culverts 
under driveways; see Chapter 1300. 
 
617.4 Turn Lane Requirements 
Turn lanes and additional right-of-way may be required on collectors and 
arterials as required by the County and a Traffic Study. Factors to consider 
when performing a warrant study include shoulder width, percentage of 
trucks, sight distance, highway grade, horizontal and vertical curvature, 
and crash histor y. Turn lane lengths shall be determined on a case -by-
case basis and shall be approved by the County. Turn lanes may be a 
condition of issuance for the access permit. 
 
617.4.1 Left Turn Lanes 
A 12-foot-wide left turn lane with appropriate storage and transitions shall 
be provided at each driveway where inbound peak hour left turning traffic 
is 30 vehicles or more. This requirement may be waived when the speed 
and volume of the opposing traffic is not sufficient to require a left turn 
lane, as determined by the County Engineer or designee. Alternately, the 
County Engineer or designee may require a left turn lane in cases with 
less than 30 left turn vehicles in the peak hour where the mix of vehicles, 
speeds and/or volumes on the street create a safety hazard.

617.4.2 Right Turn Lanes 
A 12 -foot-wide right turn lane with appropriate storage and transitions 
shall be provided at each driveway where the street average daily traffic 
volumes exceed 10,000 vehicles per day and driveway volume exceeds 
1,000 trips per day or 75 right turns inbound in the peak hour. Alternately, 
the County Engineer or designee may require a right tur n lane in cases 
with less than 75 left turn vehicles in the peak hour where the mix of 
vehicles, speeds and/or volumes on the street create a safety hazard.

617.5 Driveway Categories 
 
617.5.1 Residential Driveways 
A residential driveway is one providing access to a single -family 
residence, a duplex, or an apartment building containing 5 or fewer 
dwelling units. Residential lots with frontage of 100 feet or more, the 
County may allow an additional driveway if site conditions allow.  In new 
subdivisions, all driveways shall be a consistent configuration and 
material throughout the development, subject to County approval. 
 
New residential driveways on parcels that have potential access to two 
(2) different roadways (e.g., corner lots), the access shall be on the street 
with the lower classification. Parcel access shall be from a local road 
rather than a collector or arterial to maintain higher speeds on busier 
roadways. In cases where a property faces both a public and private road, 
the County the County requires access from the private road.  
 
Residential parcels that only front onto arterial or collector street shall 
have a single access point if there are no reasonable alternate public 
access points available, as determined by the County. If such access is 
permitted, the driveway shall be either circular or have a designated turn-
around area to prevent vehicles from needi ng to reverse onto the street. 
Refer to ADOT Standard Drawing No. C -06.10 for vertical profile 
recommendations.

617.5.2 Multifamily Residential 
Multifamily residential is defined as either: 
1. Low-volume driveway that provides access to more than three (3) 
off-street parking stalls for more than two (2) dwelling units.  
2. High-volume driveway  that provide access to more than 
50 dwelling units and are normally on a major collector or an 
arterial street. The County may allow the widening of multifamily 
driveways up to 12  feet on the egress side to accommodate a 
dedicated left-turn lane. 
 
Multifamily shall comply with the requirements shown in Table 617.5. 
 
617.5.3 Commercial and Industrial Driveways 
Commercial/industrial driveways and turnouts must consider the 
requirements of truck traffic and shall be designed using the appropriate 
turning template. The pavement surface of these driveways must be equal 
to or more durable than the connecting roadway.

617.5.3.1 Commercial Driveways 
Commercial driveways provide access to office buildings, retail stores, 
institutional building, or apartment building with more than five (5) dwelling 
units. They can function as access for service and delivery trucks, rather 
than serving as the main entra nce. Commercial driveways that primarily 
serve administrative, or employee parking lots are also classified as 
commercial driveways. 
 
617.5.3.2 Industrial Driveways 
Industrial driveways serve a large volume of truck traffic going to and from 
loading docks at industrial sites, warehouses, or truck terminals. In the 
case of centralized retail developments like community regional shopping 
centers, there may be specific driveways designated, marke d, and 
positioned to accommodate truck access. These driveways are 
considered industrial driveways as well. 
 
617.5.4 Temporary Access 
Temporary access may be granted to undeveloped property prior to 
development of a final plan if access is needed for construction or 
preliminary site access. Temporary access shall require a permit to the 
undeveloped property prior to development of the final plan and is subject 
to removal, relocation, or redesign after final development plan approval. 
 
617.6 Guidelines for Primitive Roads 
Primitive roads do not follow “typical” roadway design standards however 
when used for public or commercial use, designers should consult the 
AASHTO Green Book , Chapter 5 and  the AASHTO Guidelines for 
Geometric Design of Very Low-Volume Local Roads.  
 
617.7 Cross Section 
1. Typically, does not conform to County standards. 
2. May have inconsistent width, but roads must have minimum widths 
to safely operate equipment for blading, typically a 12 -foot (single 
lane) travel width. 
3. Surface varies from native material to rock and gravel. 
4. Surface must be in a maintainable state when designed by the 
County as a Primitive Road.

617.7.1 Backslopes 
Make the primitive roads backslope as steep as the soil material will stand, 
without causing serious erosion. While most soils will stand with a ½:1 
(H:V) or ¾:1 (H:V) backslope, this is not always true over time. Be careful 
to use an angle of repose that will maintain a stable condition indefinitely. 
 
617.8 Clearing 
Primitive roads should be cleared of all projecting limbs, brush, down logs, 
and debris that endanger a prudent user. In sparely timbered country, do 
not remove any healthy trees unless they interfere with traffic, and the 
primitive road cannot be relocated to eliminate the interference. 
 
617.9 Drainage 
Proper drainage is critical in primitive road design. Protection of the travel 
way, adjacent upstream and downstream lands depend upon proper 
drainage design. This requires basic knowledge of both hydrology and 
hydraulics. The design of primitive roads may include the use of culverts, 
ditches, water bars, and other drainage elements to handle runoff and 
protect adjacent land from environmental damage. 
  
Provide for surface drainage with grade dips and out sloping. Provide 
cross drainage with water bars, ditching, built -up rock, and culverts as 
needed. In designing a grade for a section of primitive road, leave 
sufficient “slack” to permit grade dips at pr oper intervals without making 
the intervening sections steeper than the recommended maximum grade. 
Stake the exact location, length, and configuration of the dips in the field 
prior to commencing earthwork. Do not overlook the control of water at 
the discharge points. Employ rocks and native materials to dissipate water 
and controlling erosion when in plentiful supply.  
 
617.9.1 Fords 
Fords may be required to minimize damage to the stream channels. 
 
617.10 Earthwork Design 
Although not of primary importance, the County encourages balanced 
design for primitive roads. Waste is discouraged unless soil 
characteristics are unsuitable for vehicle loads. Limit borrow to surfacing 
materials where needed. Adjust alignment, gradient, or slopes to minimize 
the need for waste or borrow.

617.11 Alignment 
Alignment of primitive roads should consider elements such as 
surrounding terrain, grade, cross slope, and sight distance. Installation of 
turnouts on primitive roads are recommended when feasible. See the 
AASHTO Green Book, Chapter 5, Sections 5.4 to 5.6 and  the AASHTO 
Guidelines for Geometric Design of Very Low-Volume Local Roads. 
 
617.11.1 Turnouts 
Turnouts are best located on points, in gullies, or ravines. Turnouts may 
be field adjusted to take advantage of points and ravines. Turnouts should 
be intervisible on steep, single lane segments. See the AASHTO Green 
Book, Figure 5-5 for turnout design. 
 
617.11.2 Grade Dips 
Grade dips are sections where a short area of road, generally not 
exceeding 8 to 10 feet long, is built with a grade slightly adverse to the 
prevailing grade of the route segment. This prevents the flowing water 
from passing that point. The road is out slo ped at the lowest point in the 
dip to divert the water from the travel way. Grade dips are the most 
satisfactory when built in the original construction and the designed grade 
allows for the adverse section to be built in a cut section. 
 
617.12 Erosion Control 
Erosion control is an important consideration on steep slopes. Erosion 
control is required when constructing steep cut slopes or embankments 
in erosive soils. Erosion control can be permanent (rock, fabrics, grids, 
concrete) or temporary (straw mats, hay bales, brush piles or plantings). 
 
617.13 Soil Survey and Material Site Investigation 
The extent of survey and sampling and testing work required depends on 
the type and size of the project and the character of the soils. Visual 
classification is sufficient for most primitive roads. Use the Unified Soil 
Classification system to perform visu al soil investigations and 
classifications. 
 
617.14 Warning Signs 
Roads designated as primitive, by the County, shall have warning signs 
placed in locations to adequately warn the public. Signs shall conform to 
the following requirements:

619 Cattle Guards 
Cattle guards, with or without gates, may be required to prevent livestock 
from interfering with roadway traffic or to maintain range control. To 
prevent livestock from entering the Right-of-Way, the construction of cattle 
guards may be required at side ro ads or private entrances. Install cattle 
guards based on ADOT Detail C-11.10.

unless otherwise approved by the County Engineer. Design, construct 
and maintain p avement surfaces at railroad crossings to permit safe, 
smooth crossings for all roadway users. Install w arning signs and 
pavement markings in accordance with  ADOT’s Signing and Marking 
Standards and  the MUTCD. Permits from railroad and state agencies 
must be issued prior to County approvals or acceptance.

700 Introduction 
It is the intent of the County to have a comprehensive storm water 
management program that protects the health, safety and welfare of its 
citizens, their property, and the environment. The County’s storm water 
management documents may be accessed using the  Quick Links and 
include the following: 
• County Ordinance 01-16 Flood Damage Prevention (2016)  
• County Subdivision Regulations 
o County Drainage, Section 3.10 
o County Drainage Policy, Section 3.15 
 
700.1 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose of this Chapter is to provide developers, engineers, and 
builders involved in projects within the County with comprehensive 
information and guidance on drainage design. The aim of these policies 
and guidelines is to ensure that proper drainage practices are followed. 
In cases where there are conflicts between any code and ordinance, the 
stricter regulations will take precedence. 
 
This Chapter is intended to assist in the design and assessment of both 
public and private stormwater management facilities within Navajo 
County, Arizona. It includes guidelines for stormwater management 
policies, design procedures, and criteria for conduc ting hydrologic and 
hydraulic studies, designs, and evaluations. While the objective is to 
promote consistent design practices, it is important to acknowledge that 
engineering judgment is necessary, and alternative methods may be 
considered with approval from the County. 
 
The overall goals for the development of this manual are to: 
1. Compliance with applicable floodplain and stormwater 
management regulations, policies, and design criteria. 
2. Minimize public expenditures for drainage projects. 
3. Minimize the review time of drainage report and/or grading and 
drainage plan submittals. 
4. Provide consistent policies and criteria that will result in uniform 
practices and drainage infrastructure within the County. 
5. Improve the water quality of stormwater runoff within the County.

The owner, developer, engineer, or contractor must obtain and adhere 
to the permit requirements of other relevant agencies, even if they 
comply with the requirements stated in this Manual. 
 
700.2 Legal Authority 
Navajo County, a governmental entity within the State of Arizona, is 
prohibited from issuing any permit(s) that would lead to an adverse 
alteration of the volume, velocity, flooding extents or direction of water 
flow entering or exiting adjacent properties during construction or 
improvement activities. To obtain a permit from the County, property 
owners or their representatives must first secure written approval from 
the County. In cases where engineering analysis is necessary for permit 
approval, the engineer's report and construction plans must adhere to 
the guidelines outlined in this Manual. 
 
700.3 Requirements and Applicability 
All developments within the County must include storm drainage facilities 
to protect all improvements, structures, and properties from the negative 
effects of storm water caused by the proposed development. The design 
and construction of these facilities should ensure that the flow of wate r 
after development is not greater than the flow before development for 
various flood events. 
 
For any development or construction project in the County, it is required 
to prepare and submit a Drainage Plan and a Drainage Report. 
Additional reports and documentation may be necessary as per the 
County Subdivision Regulations when submitting a Tentative Plat. 
 
Prepare and submit a Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) 
for any development/construction project greater than one (1) acre, or as 
required to comply with ADEQ and EPA regulations. Prior to 
commencing construction, provide a copy of the Notice of Intent (NOI) 
filed with ADEQ to the County. 
  
Submit all required permit applications to appropriate federal or state 
agencies for any development or project impacting the "Waters of the 
United States", as per Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, or a 
designated floodplain according to the U.S. Federal  Emergency 
Management Agency, or ADWR. Submit proof of permit acquisition to 
the County.

These standards represent the minimum requirements. If the application 
of the minimum standard could potentially harm public health, safety, and 
welfare, more rigorous requirements may be imposed. The information 
provided is based on accepted engineering p rocedures and criteria, but 
the specific applicability of these criteria to a particular project must be 
confirmed by an Arizona Registered Professional Civil Engineer. 
 
700.4 References 
Refer to the following documents for drainage design and reports in the 
County: 
• ADOT Roadway Design Guidelines, Chapter 600 
• ADOT Drainage Design Manual, Volume 2, Hydrology, including 
Appendices and Hydrology Data and Application Downloads 
• ADOT Highway Drainage Design Manual, Hydraulics 
• Navajo County Flood Insurance Study (FIS) 
 
Where certain exclusions, modification, or supplements to the sections 
of the adopted manuals are required, they are stated within the specific 
chapter of this Manual. Seek clarification from the County if a subsequent 
update conflicts with this Manual. 
 
In ADOT manuals, guidelines, or reports, the term "ADOT" should be 
substituted with the County when mentioned. 
 
700.5 Deviation from Adopted Standards 
The County Engineer or designee has the authority to grant a Waiver 
permitting variations from these guidelines based on the criteria specified 
in the Waiver Request Form. Before the Engineering Plans are approved 
for construction, any known deviations must be approved. 
 
701 Drainage Reports 
Drainage reports and/or engineered grading and drainage plans are 
required to: 
1. Analyze the impact that the proposed development or project will 
have on stormwater discharges; 
2. Provide adequate data to ensure that the development is 
designed to be protected from flooding and conforms to applicable 
floodplain and stormwater management regulations;

3. Provide data for the design of public and private drainage 
facilities. 
 
Ensure that drainage reports contain thorough details to show that the 
development or project will not result in drainage or flooding issues, and 
that any on-site drainage systems are adequately designed to handle the 
expected storm flows. 
 
701.1 Applicability Requirements 
The following land development activities require drainage reports: 
• Residential, commercial, and industrial subdivisions. 
• Any multi-family residential or commercial development, parking 
lot or park. 
• Application for rezoning in conjunction with a qualifying 
development project. 
• Public improvements involving new streets, culverts, storm drains, 
open channels, and private/public detention facilities or other 
drainage infrastructure. 
• Application for Conditional Letter of Map Revision (CLOMR) or 
Letter of Map Revision (LOMR) to the Federal Emergency 
Management Agency (FEMA). 
• Any other improvements which, in the opinion of the County, 
require a report. 
 
The following applications may require a drainage report: 
• Building permit 
• Floodplain use permit 
• Grading permit  
• Site conditions warrant or if, in the opinion of the County, drainage 
issues affect the development of the site. 
 
Drainage reports that are submitted to the County for review and 
approval must be prepared and sealed by an Arizona Registered 
Professional Civil Engineer who exhibits expertise in the particular field 
of design. Adhere to the drainage report guidelines ou tlined in this 
Manual for either Phase I or Phase II criteria. 
 
The County recommends a pre -drainage submittal meeting before 
preparing or submitting drainage items.

701.1.1 Subdivision Drainage Studies 
Analyze all drainage basins within a tributary area at the point that they 
enter the subdivision or confluence within the subdivision. 
 
The County may approve adjustments to the size limitation of different 
delineations based on the conditions of the specific subdivision. In cases 
where channelization of an existing drainageway is suggested, it is 
essential to conduct both pre -development and post -development 
analyses to demonstrate the impacts of the proposed enhancements. 
 
Submit a Phase I Drainage Report at the time of the Tentative Plat 
Review; see Section 701.3 for additional information. 
 
701.1.2 Rezoning Applications 
All development projects must address how stormwater will be managed 
during construction. Drainage reports and plans addressing the 
stormwater management must be submitted in conjunction with rezoning 
applications. Most rezoning applications will require submittal of a Phase 
I Drainage Report (See Section 701.3). Detailed hydrologic and hydraulic 
analyses will not be required for most rezoning applications, unless the 
County determines that the site drainage is a limiting factor in the 
successful development of the subject site. 
 
701.2 Floodplain Studies and Map Revisions 
Detailed floodplain studies (i.e., Technical Data Support Notebooks) are 
required for the following applications to FEMA: 
• Conditional Letter of Map Revision (CLOMR) 
• Letter of Map Revision (LOMR) 
• Physical Map Revision (PMR) 
• Floodplain studies may also be required by the County Engineer 
for the following: 
o Conditional Letter of Map Amendment (CLOMA) 
o Conditional Letter of Map Revision Based on Fill 
(CLOMR-F) 
 
Prior to submitting to FEMA, it is required for the County to review all 
FEMA applications. Refer to the County Floodplain Overlay for locations 
to identify where FEMA applications may be required. Additionally, the 
County may require flood studies for any other development(s) that may 
adversely affect floodplain depths.

701.2.1 General Guidelines 
Prepare FEMA map revision requests for hydraulic models as follows: 
1. Duplicate Effective Model (natural and floodway models, when 
available) 
a. Using the same computer program (e.g., HEC -2, HEC -
RAS), run the model on your computer and check the result 
with the output to make sure the model was duplicated. 
b. Assures the baseline is correct and the revised model will 
tie back into the effective model upstream of the revised 
reach. 
2. Corrected Effective Model 
a. Using a newer version of the same program 
b. More detailed cross sections that reflect conditions that 
existed when the original model was developed. 
c. Fix technical errors. 
d. An improved computer model or improved bridge routine 
e. Add bridges, culverts, or other structures that existed but 
were not modeled. 
f. Becomes the new base model to measure impacts of 
development/construction. 
3. Existing Conditions Model 
a. Update the corrected effective model to include existing 
conditions natural changes in the floodplain. 
b. Reflects fill in the floodway fringe since original model was 
developed, and other channel improvements. 
c. Other bridges and culverts 
d. Used as baseline model to measure the effects solely 
attributed to the “project" as reflected by the post -project 
model. 
4. Post-Project Model 
a. Reflects the project (built or proposed) and determines the 
impacts of the project. 
 
701.3 Drainage Report Requirements 
Conform to current FEMA requirements for a required floodway analysis.

701.3.1 Drainage Statement 
A Drainage Statement must be included in the plans and submitted as a 
memorandum for projects that are unaffected by significant offsite flows 
or have been approved by the County Engineer, to show that the site is 
not impacted by any offsite flows. 
 
For sites with drainage basin areas of 160-acres or less in size, use the 
Rational Method for calculations. For sites with drainage basins greater 
than 160 -acres in size, provide the methodology used for calculating 
bandwidths for flows and flow rates.  
 
701.3.2 Phase I Drainage Report 
The Phase I Report will review, on a conceptual level, the feasibility and 
design characteristics of the proposed development or project. Print the 
Phase I Drainage Report on 8.5" x 11” paper (except drainage maps) 
and be properly bound. Submit an electron ic version of the report and 
models. The report shall be in accordance with the following outline and 
contain at a minimum the applicable information listed.

wastewater treatment and disposal system

701.3.3 Phase II Drainage Report 
The Phase II Drainage Report serves to identify and define specific 
solutions for potential on -site and off -site issues that may arise due to 
development. Furthermore, any existing drainage concerns on-site must 
be resolved prior to development. 
 
Submit Phase II Drainage Reports in conjunction with Final Plat 
applications and Commercial Projects. Submit a ll reports on 8.5” x 11” 
paper (excluding drainage maps) and securely bound. Submit a n 
electronic copy of the report and models. Drawings, computer disks, 
figures, plates, and tables must be bound together with the report. 
Include a report cover letter detailing the final design for review, prepared 
by or under the supervision of an Arizona Registered Professional Civil 
Engineer. A signed and sealed  certification sheet is required  with the 
following statement: 
 
"This report and drainage plan for the Phase II drainage design of 
(Name of Development) was prepared by me (or under my direct 
supervision) in accordance with the provisions of the drainage 
planning submittal requirements of Navajo County and other 
regulations of the Navajo County Flood Control District (NCFCD). 
I understand that Navajo County does not, and will not, assume 
liability for the calculations, design elements, or drainage facilities 
designed by others."

701.4 Submittal Requirements 
All drainage report and plan submittals submitted to the County for 
review shall be prepared and sealed by an Arizona Registered 
Professional Civil Engineer who demonstrates proficiency in the specific 
area of design. 
 
The engineer is solely responsible for the accuracy and sufficiency of all 
data, drawings, calculations, and reports submitted to the County for 
review and approval. In addition, the engineer shall comply with all 
floodplain regulations at the local, state , and federal levels when 
designing a development. 
 
The County will review drainage report and plan submittals for 
completeness and overall compliance with all applicable local, state, and 
federal requirements. Approval by the County does not necessarily 
indicate that the design is appropriate, nor that the  development is in 
strict compliance with all applicable regulations and standards. Review 
and approval of drainage submittals does not hold the County or its staff 
responsible for any flood-related damages that may occur due to reliance 
on administrative decisions made by the County or its employees.

702.3 Modifications and Deviations 
 
702.3.1 Review and Approval 
County review and approv al is required in all cases where the ADOT 
Hydrology Manual mandates review and approval. 
 
702.3.2 Requirements for Drainage Reports 
A comprehensive description of the requirements and methodologies for 
documenting hydrologic and hydraulic analyses is in Section 701. 
 
702.3.3 Minimum Time of Concentration (Tc) 
When estimating rainfall intensity, it is recommended to use a minimum 
Time of Concentration (Tc) of 10 minutes. However, there are cases 
where a shorter Tc may be more suitable and may be required by the 
County Engineer. A Tc less than 5 minutes is not permitted under any 
circumstances. 
 
702.3.4 Selection of Runoff Coefficient (C) 
There may be instances in the County where a custom runoff coefficient 
(C) that differs from the curves provided in the ADOT Hydrology Manual 
may be more appropriate. 
 
In all cases where a custom runoff coefficient (C) is used, a justification 
for this value must be provided and documented, along with a thorough 
comparison to the existing runoff coefficients (C) in the ADOT Hydrology 
Manual. County approval is required for all custom runoff coefficients (C). 
 
702.3.5 Rainfall Losses 
 
702.3.5.1 Green and Ampt Loss Rate Method 
The County prefers to use the Green and Ampt Loss rate method with 
the Unit Hydrograph methodology. However, when estimating surface 
retention loss, follow the ADOT Hydrology Manual methodology, with the 
exception that Table 3 -1 Surface Retention Loss (Max Storage) for 
Various Land Surfaces in Arizona should be replaced with the following

702.3.5.2 Initial and Constant Loss 
The County discourages the use of the initial and constant loss method 
for rainfall losses, although it is permitted. This method may be suitable 
for areas with high infiltration rates. However, if the initial and constant 
loss method is employed, it is mandatory to conduct soil testing, calibrate 
the model, and compare it to the Green and Ampt methodology. 
Additionally, a comprehensive justification and documentation must be 
provided to support the use of this method. Approval from the County 
Engineer or t heir representative is required for any application of the 
initial and constant loss method. 
 
702.3.6 Transmission Losses 
As a general rule, t ransmission losses are prohibited . However, if the 
project site is expected to be significantly affected by transmission 
losses, it is necessary to obtain County approval before implementing 
such losses. Additionally, any utilization of transmission losses may 
necessitate soil testing and model calibration. To proceed with the use 
of transmission losses, it is imperative to provide comprehensive 
justification and documentation. 
 
702.3.7 Regression Equations 
Use USGS Streamstats for verification and calibration. 
 
702.3.8 Indirect Methods for Discharge Verification 
The ADOT Hydrology Manual does not provide any further guidance on 
methods for verifying and calibrating discharges, apart from the use of 
regional regression equations. To ensure the accuracy of hydrologic 
analysis, verify all discharge calculations using  the StreamStats tool 
provided by the USGS.  
 
This process utilizes three indirect procedures for verification, and in 
general, all three procedures should be followed. They include the 
following: 
1. A graph of numerous peak discharges versus drainage area 
curves 
2. A graph of estimated 100 -year discharges and maximum 
recorded discharges versus drainage area for gaged watersheds 
in Arizona 
3. Regression equations and data graphs for flood regions in the 
County

702.3.9 Watersheds above 7000 Feet 
When watersheds are located above 7000 feet, the engineer shall take 
into account the possibility of rain falling on snow or frozen ground when 
calculating stormwater runoff. The engineer shall document and justify 
the procedures utilized in the Drainage R eport. An example of 
justification would be analyzing local gauges and identifying when 
seasonal peak discharges occur for a specific area.

4. Typical section street cross slopes shall not be decreased or 
increased, and curb heights shall not be increased to create more 
carrying capacity for runoff. Curb overtopping is not permitted for 
the 10-year design storm. 
5. Public streets with inverted crowns are prohibited. 
6. Existing alleys shall not be used to convey runoff unless the entire 
alley is designed and constructed to convey runoff to the nearest 
downstream street. 
7. Drainage facilities shall be placed to intercept runoff from sources 
outside the street section to avoid concentrated flows onto and 
over sidewalks or curb and gutter. 
8. In all cases, confine street drainage to the public right -of-way. 
Runoff which leaves the right -of-way shall do so in a controlled 
manner and shall be conveyed in an appropriate tract or drainage 
easement. 
 
703.2.3.1 Design Frequency and Allowable Spread 
Confine the runoff from the 10-year design storm within the curbs of local 
street sections, while the 100 -year flow must be contained within the 
right- of-way. 
 
At least one travel lane in each direction on collector and arterial curbed 
street sections must be kept clear of flooding for the 10 -year design 
storm, with the 100 -year flow contained within the right-of-way. If either 
criterion is not met, the installation of storm drain facilities is required. 
Furthermore, the 10-year design storm must always be contained within 
the combined street gutter and storm drain system. 
 
703.2.3.2 Catch Basin Selection 
Catch basin inlets for use within the right-of-way, an easement, or public 
property shall be per MAG Details. Slotted drain inlets are only permitted 
for special circumstances, as approved by the County Engineer, where 
standard drainage inlets will not suf fice. Slotted drain inlets on a 
longitudinal grade function best when designed and constructed in 
conjunction with a curb opening inlet and when debris is not a factor. 
Slotted inlets for public storm drains are not permitted in sump locations 
due to high clogging potential and sediment deposition problems in the 
pipe section.

703.2.3.4 Roadside Ditches and Channels 
Design roadside ditches or channels for rural, uncurbed street sections 
for a 25 -year design storm. Contain the runoff within the roadside 
channels with the allowable water depth elevation below the roadway 
subgrade to avoid unnecessary saturation of the s ubgrade and/or 
aggregate base course shoulder. Design the minimum depth of a 
roadside channel to be at least 1.5 feet below subgrade. See the typical 
sections in the Standard Details for additional information. Only roadway 
drainage and drainage from areas immediately adjacent to the roadway 
shall be carried in roadside drainage channels.

Local soil conditions, flow depths, and velocities within the channel are 
typically the main hydraulic factors in channel geometric design . 
However, terrain and safety have considerable influence. Steeper side 
slopes of rigid, lined channels can offer cost -effective solutions and 
enhance hydraulic flow characteristics. The application of steeper slopes 
is generally restricted to areas with limited right -of-way, where traffic 
hazards can be mitigated by using barriers. It is preferable to avoid the 
use of long stretches of riprap lined roadside channels to prevent long-
term maintenance issues. 
 
703.3 Storm Drains & Culverts 
 
703.3.1 Installation, Details and Specifications 
Install all drainage features, including storm drains, culverts, manholes, 
junction structure, catch basins, inlets, outlets, aprons, and other related 
features, in accordance with the following ADOT and MAG documents: 
• ADOT Standard Specifications 
• ADOT Standard Details (C-Stds) 
• ADOT Structure Detail Drawings (SD-Stds) 
• ADOT Approved Products List, if applicable 
• MAG Specifications and Details  
 
703.3.2 Storm Drain and Culvert Material Selection 
Various factors, including longevity, strength, cover depth, joint integrity, 
hydraulic efficiency, ease of use, installation expenses, and upkeep, 
must all be taken into account when choosing storm drain  and culvert 
materials to optimize both performance and cost efficiency.  
 
Corrugated Metal is required. A waiver request may be submitted to use 
alternate pipe materials such as, Smooth Steel, Reinforced Concrete or 
HDPE. Do not use HDPE in fire susceptible areas. All pipes shall conform 
to ADOT’s Standard Specifications and be on ADOT’s Approved 
Products List. Refer to ADOT’s Pipe Selection Guidelines and Roadway 
Design Guidelines.

703.3.3 Maintenance Considerations 
It is essential to take maintenance into account throughout the design 
and construction of storm drain systems and culverts. Typical 
maintenance issues related to storm drains and culverts include debris 
accumulation, sediment buildup, scouring, pipe block ages, settling of 
roads or embankments, and structural deterioration of the pipe. The 
potential for scouring and abrasion within the pipe should be factored in 
during the process. Furthermore, provisions for easy access for 
inspection and maintenance of st orm drains and drainage inlets should 
be included in the planning. 
 
Clearing accumulated debris and sediment from storm drain, culverts, 
inlets, and outlets is an essential maintenance obligation for every facility 
owner. Nevertheless, this issue is frequently overlooked during 
construction, and it is crucial to take appropriate precautions for 
sediment/erosion control. 
 
Settlement issues in piping, roadways, or embankments, as well as 
structural damage, are often linked to substandard construction 
methods. These problems can be prevented by implementing 
appropriate design, installation guidelines, and regular inspections. 
 
703.3.4 Manholes and Junction Structures 
 
703.3.4.1 Location and Spacing 
The primary purpose of establishing criteria for manhole location and 
spacing is to meet the maintenance needs of storm drains or culverts. To 
ensure proper functionality, manholes are mandatory in the following 
areas: 
1. At junctions where two or more storm drains or culverts converge 
(not including laterals from adjacent catch basins) 
2. At storm drain vertical deflections 
3. Changes in pipe size 
4. At storm drain horizontal alignment changes as outlined below:

703.3.4.2 Manhole Configurations 
For storm drains or culverts measuring 36 inches and above, utilize a 
vertical riser or prefabricated "tee" to connect to the storm drain, subject

Use a pressure manhole shaft, pressure frame, and cover if the design

accordance with ADOT Standard Detail C-18.10.

Manhole depths shall be determined based on the storm drain or culvert 
profile and surface topography, typically ranging from 5 to 13 feet. 
Manholes that are either shallower or deeper may require special design 
considerations. Deep manholes (exceeding 12 feet), a diameter of 
60 inches is required to withstand pressures. Additionally, if a manhole 
extends below the water table, it must be designed to withstand 
hydrostatic pressure and/or seepage. Manhole shafts should have a 
diameter of 60 inches for storm drain pipes or culverts 36 inches in 
diameter or larger. 
 
703.3.4.3 Manhole Shaping 
A minimum drop of 0.10-foot is required through all storm drain or culvert 
manholes. For a manhole with two contributing laterals a drop of 0.3 feet 
is preferred, if possible. In cases where a storm drain or culvert changes 
within a manhole, a drop of 0.4 feet is preferred, if possible to maintain 
positive flow through the manhole.  
 
703.4 Storm Drain Design 
1. All offsite runoff from whatever source must be considered in the 
design of a storm drain system if such runoff could affect the street 
that the storm drain is serving. 
2. Storm drain systems serving collector and arterial streets must 
keep one 12 -foot lane of traffic open in each direction for the 
10-year design storm and the 100 -year storm within the right -of-
way. Storm drain systems for local streets must keep the 10-year 
design flow between the curbs. 
3. The minimum design frequency for all public storm drain facilities 
shall be the 10 -year design storm. The 100 -year design storm 
must also be analyzed to ensure that the 100 -year storm is 
maintained within the right-of-way. 
4. The minimum easement width for public storm drains 36 inches in 
diameter or less shall be 16 feet. For multiple pipe installations or 
pipe diameter greater than 36 inches, the easement width shall 
be the conduit width(s) plus 8 feet on each side of the con duit 
measured from its edge. 
5. The minimum acceptable diameter for any public storm drain pipe 
is 18 inches. Mainline storm drains shall be at least 24 inches in 
diameter. 
6. New storm drains and manholes shall not run longitudinally under 
existing or future curb and gutter or sidewalk, whenever possible.

703.4.1 Design Velocity and Slope 
Storm drain pipe shall have a minimum slope of 0.5 percent or a slope 
that generates a velocity of 3 feet per second when the pipe is flowing 
full, whichever is greater. Approval from the County is required for slopes 
less than 0.5 percent. 
 
The desirable minimum velocity is 5 feet per second, but it essential that 
all storm drains are designed to maintain a minimum self -cleaning 
velocity of 3 feet per second when flowing at full capacity. Use Equation 
703-1 to calculate the minimum slope required to achieve a velocity of 
3 feet per second in storm drains. 
 
Equation 703-1 Minimum Slope based on Velocity 
  
It is important to take note of the following flow conditions at various 
depths within a circular pipe: 
1. Peak flow occurs at 93 percent of the height of the pipe. This 
means that if a pipe is designed for full flow, the design will be 
slightly conservative. 
2. The velocity in a pipe flowing half -full is the same as the velocity 
for full flow. 
3. Flow velocities for surcharged storm drains with hydraulic grade 
line elevations above the top of pipe (pressure flow) are greater 
than velocities at full flow. 
4. As the depth of flow drops below half -full, the flow velocity drops 
off rapidly.

703.4.2 Alignment 
Storm drains should be designed straight, with uniform slopes between 
manholes. However, in cases where conforming to the street layout 
requires it, curved storm drains with long radius bends many be allowed. 
Note that storm drains smaller than 4 feet in d iameter should not be 
designed with curves. For storm drains that are 4 feet in diameter or 
larger, long radius bends are recommended as a preferred methods for 
changing direction, unless a manhole is necessary. The specified radius 
of curvature should ali gn with the standard curves available for the 
specific type of material used. The minimum radius shall not be less than 
100 feet. 
 
703.4.3 Storm Drain Size 
Lateral pipes for public storm drains shall have a minimum diameter of 
18 inches, while mainline shall have a minimum diameter of 24 inches. 
Approval from the County is required for the use of elliptical or arched 
pipe for storm drains. The size of storm d rain pipe shall progressively 
increase in the downstream direction. Decreasing the pipe size in the 
downstream direction, even if the flow is on a steeper slope or for 
pressure profiles is not permitted. 
 
703.4.4 Separation Requirements 
Installation and backfill requirements for public storm drains shall be in 
accordance with ADOT Specifications and Details. 
 
The vertical and horizontal separation criteria for storm drain pipes and 
waterlines shall conform to the standards set for sewer pipes as outlined 
in this Manual. 
 
The required distance between storm drains and any other dry 
underground utilities shall conform to the standards set for  sewer pipes 
as outlined in this Manual. Whenever feasible, utility crossings should be 
made at angles exceeding 45 degrees. 
 
Extra depth, concrete encasement, channel stabilization, or other 
protective measures may be necessary for crossings of open channels 
in order to prevent scour.
