703.4.5 Storm Drain Outfalls 
All storm drain systems are required to have a point of discharge, where 
the flow is released into either a natural watercourse, artificial channel, 
another storm drain system, or any other drainage facility. Various 
factors related to the design of storm drain outlets need to be taken into 
account, such as the invert of the outlet, tailwater elevation(s), type of 
receiving watercourse, orientation of the outlet, and local scour. 
 
If the discharge point is a wash or stream, it is essential to consider the 
simultaneous likelihood of two hydrologic events happening. There may 
be situations where excessive downstream water causes the flow to 
reverse in the storm drain system and potentially lead to overflowing 
inlets and manholes. It is recommended to have the bottom of the storm 
drain outlet at least 1 -foot higher than the bottom of the channel at the 
same location. 
 
The evaluation of the hydraulic grade line necessitates careful 
consideration of the tailwater depth at the storm drain outlet. 
 
Storm drains discharging into open channels shall have a 
headwall/wingwall, with no projecting outlets allowed. The outlet 
orientation should be downstream to minimize turbulence and local 
scour. If the outlet is perpendicular to the flow direction, erosion of the 
opposite bank must be taken into account, potentially requiring a riprap 
lining. An energy dissipater might be necessary for high outlet velocities. 
 
703.5 Culvert Design 
Culverts typically convey storm water through an embankment or acting 
main discharge point for detention facilities. They are typically aligned 
with natural washes, watercourses, or open channels that function the 
primary outfall for local and regional dra inageways. The design of 
culverts takes into account factors such as their intended use, hydraulic 
effectiveness, site topography, impacts on adjacent property, and cost. 
 
To ensure the pipe's structural integrity under expected loading 
conditions, it is necessary to have a minimum amount of fill covering the 
culverts. All culverts should have at least 24 inches of cover from the 
finished elevation to the top of the pipe , except at driveways where at 
least 12 inches of cover may be used. Under no circumstances shall the 
culverts extend into the roadway base. If it is not possible to meet the

703.5.1 Design Velocity and Slope 
The culvert must maintain a minimum velocity of 3 feet per second when 
it is flowing partially full.

703.5.3 Pipe Collars 
Install pipe collars at all horizontal and vertical alignment changes of a 
culvert. Manholes may be utilized instead of pipe collars upon receiving 
approval from the County. 
 
703.5.4 Minimum Cover 
In the design of roadway culverts, it is crucial to take into account both 
the minimum and maximum cover limits. The minimum cover limits are 
set to guarantee the structural stability of the culvert when subjected to 
live and impact loads. As the fill heig ht increases, dead loads become 
the determining factor.  Designers shall refer to ADOT’s Pipe Design 
Information for the Pipe Selection Guidelines and Procedures and Plastic 
Pipe Selection Guidelines as well as ADOT’s Approved Product List, 
Standard Specifications, and Roadway Design Guidelines. 
 
Culverts ranging from 18 to 36 inches in diameter shall have a minimum 
cover of 2 feet from the top of the pipe to the top of the top of finished 
grade. For culverts larger than 36 inches in diameter, the minimum cover 
should be 30 percent of the culvert diameter, if feasible. It is crucial that 
the top of any culvert does not protrude above the roadway subgrade 
within the roadway street section. 
 
703.5.5 Inlets and Outlets 
Whenever feasible, culvert inlets should align with the shape of the 
roadway embankment. To minimize headwater elevations, enhance the

703.5.6 Reinforced Concrete Box Culvert (RCB) 
Reinforced Concrete Box Culverts (RCB) shall have a minimum height 
of 4 feet, a desirable height of 6 feet, and a minimum width of 6 feet.

shall be designed to convey the 100 -year event runoff under the road

704.1 Low Water Crossings 
Low water crossings or vented fords may be permitted in locations with 
shallow or distributary flow, provided that the County determines that a 
culvert or bridge crossing is not feasible and the following design criteria 
are satisfied: 
1. The maximum water depth crossing the roadway travel lanes for 
the 100-year peak discharge does not exceed 12 inches, and 
2. The velocity does not exceed 8 feet per second (ft/s), and 
3. Low water crossing surfaces are to be constructed per MAG 
Standard Detail 552 (Concrete Surface) or comparable all -
weather surface as approved by the County, and 
4. The crossing accesses a single-family home development. 
 
A waiver process is available for individual parcel applicants interested 
in single-family type developments who believe a culvert, bridge, or low 
water crossing as described above is not feasible. The exemption waiver 
must outline how meeting these criteria would be challenging, such as: 
1. Is financially impractical, and/or 
2. Would significantly change historical flow patterns or would result 
in significant adverse impacts to properties. 
 
If waived, the applicant must provide a notarized letter, recorded as an 
addendum to the property deed at the County Recorder’s Office, that 
acknowledges the design is not in compliance with County standards. In 
the event that legal access does not permit emergency vehicles to reach 
the lots, parcels, or fractional interests, the county, along with its agents 
and employees, shall not be held liable for any damages incurred due to 
the inability of emergency vehi cles to access the said lot, parcel, or 
fractional interest. 
 
If a development is granted approval for low water roadway crossings of 
washes with a 100-year peak discharge of 500 cubic feet per second or 
greater, the County Engineer may deem it necessary to install signage,

704.2 Channels 
 
704.2.1 Open Channels 
1. All open channel designs and/or related activities shall meet the 
minimum requirements and/or design criteria for the County, 
Federal Emergency Management Agency, U.S. Army Corps of 
Engineers 404 permitting, and the Arizona Department of 
Environmental Quality, as applicable. 
2. Open channels shall be design per ADOT’s Roadway Design 
Guidelines and this Manual. 
3. Safety of the public shall be considered in the selection of location 
and cross- sectional geometry of artificial channels. 
4. The design of artificial channels shall consider the frequency and 
type of maintenance expected and make allowance for access of 
maintenance equipment. Soil cement linings are not permitted for 
open channels intended to become public and are discouraged 
for all channels due to maintenance problems. 
5. All artificial open channel drainage systems shall be designed for 
the 50 -year design storm at a minimum and checked with the 
100-year design storm to determine available freeboard, minimum 
finished floor for structure elevations adjacent to the channel, and 
the potential for flood damages. 
6. Channels shall be designed to follow natural drainage alignments 
whenever possible. Environmental impacts of modifications to 
natural channels, including disturbance of wildlife habitat, 
wetlands, and stream bank stability shall be assessed and meet 
any applicable regulations. 
7. The County may require the designer to analyze the downstream 
impacts for channels that alter the time -of-concentration and/or 
the flow attenuation of existing conditions drainageways. 
8. All channels which are to be maintained by the County must be 
dedicated to the County either in fee title or granted as drainage 
easement and must be formally accepted for maintenance by the 
County. 
9. Unless proper authorization from the County and the adjacent 
property owner(s) is obtained, open channels must enter and exit 
a site where the channel historically flowed.

10. The lining proposed for public channels must be approved by the

704.2.2 Composite Channels 
The channel lining plays a crucial role in shaping artificial channels, as it 
is one of the most influential factors in their design. Various types of 
channel linings, such as earth (natural), grass, rock, concrete, and other 
biotechnical or synthetic meas ures, are widely used. These linings can 
be employed individually or in combination to create a composite 
channel. 
 
Trapezoidal or compound cross-sections are mandatory for public open 
channels unless authorized by the County. The stability of channel side 
slopes must be maintained along the entire length and will vary based 
on the channel bank or lining material. In certain cases, a slope stability 
analysis might be necessary. For natural vegetal or earth linings, side 
slopes should not exceed 3:1 (H:V), while for ungrouted riprap lining, the 
limit is 2:1  (H:V). However, side slopes for rigid lined channels can be 
steeper, subject to the structural stability of the lining. 
 
The depth of public open channels shall be determined by computation 
of the uniform flow depth for the design discharge plus a minimum of one 
foot of freeboard. The maximum depth for artificial public channels in 
residential areas should not exceed 3 feet, including freeboard, for safety 
considerations unless approved by the County. 
 
Sediment transport requirements must be considered for conditions of 
flow below the design frequency, especially for multi -use corridors, if 
applicable. Low and high flow sections shall be considered in the design 
of channels with large cross sections and/ or a design discharge greater 
than 100-cubic feet per second. 
 
704.2.3 Natural Channels 
Natural washes or channels  that are not officially recognized as 
floodplains by the County or FEMA and run through private land should 
ideally be preserved in their natural condition upon development. Proper 
planning and design strategies must be used to protect properties 
adjacent to these natural washes/channels  from potential flooding and 
erosion typically associated with increased development . Due to the 
increased runoff resulting from development, these natural

If relocation of a natural stream channel is unavoidable, the cross-section 
shape, meander pattern, roughness, sediment transport capacity, and 
slope should conform to the existing conditions as much as practical. 
Energy dissipation may be necessary when e xisting conditions cannot 
be duplicated. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Section 404 and 
Section 401 of the Clean Water Act permitting processes may be 
required for projects affecting Waters of the U.S., such as stream 
channelization, relocation, bank sta bilization, or roadways crossings. 
County approval does not exempt compliance with applicable Federal 
and State laws. Developer shall submit a NPDES Notice of Intent form 
and Stormwater Pollution Protection Plan for all grading permit 
applications involving site disturbance exceeding one acre. 
 
Natural channels should be analyzed through field observation, surveyed 
cross-sections, and the utilization of Normal Depth/Uniform Flow 
(Manning's Equation) or step -backwater methods (preferably HEC -2 or 
HEC-RAS), as applicable. 
 
704.2.4 Velocity 
The slope of a proposed channel is typically dependent upon the natural 
topography. However, adjustments can be made by changing the 
channel’s alignment through a development, modifying the elevation of 
inflow and outflow points, or utilizing grade control. The selected channel 
configuration, alignment, and slope should result in a stable channel. 
Public channels must have a minimum slope of 0.5 percent. The 
maximum allowable velocity for open channels is 5 feet per second  
without submitting a Waiver Request and obtaining approval. 
 
Abrupt changes in channel slope shall be avoided except when 
necessary to create a desired hydraulic jump or grade control. When 
abrupt changes in slope are unavoidable, the slope changes should not 
cause the channel top width to vary by more than 15 percent. 
 
The design engineer shall consider the velocity and flow regime in the 
design and selection of materials for the channel.

704.2.5 Grade Control 
It is recommended to incorporate the use of grade control to limit channel 
slopes/velocities and avoid the necessity of channel linings at grade 
control structures. The use of alternate channel treatments, other than 
riprap, is strongly encouraged. Methods  developed by the International 
Erosion Control Association for channel protection and streambank 
stabilization are recommended. 
 
704.2.6 Channel Linings 
Artificial open channels have a wide variety of applications ranging from 
landscaping swales to large flood control facilities. The selection of the 
open channel lining type is influenced by numerous factors such as 
hydraulics, structural features, environ mental concerns, sociologic 
impact, risks and liability, maintenance, and economics.  
 
Soil cement linings are not permitted for open channels intended to 
become public and are discouraged for all channels due to maintenance 
issues. 
 
704.2.7 Maintenance 
The minimum width of fee title dedications or drainage easements for 
public open channels shall be dependent upon the top width of the 
channel, required setbacks, and the need for maintenance access roads 
adjacent to the channel. 
 
All new public open channels must have maintenance access provided 
along at least one side. The minimum width required for maintenance 
access is 12 feet. The access can be located either adjacent to the top 
of the channel bank, down into the channel bottom, or a combination of 
both. In any case, the right -of-way or drainage easement must be wide 
enough to allow maintenance vehicles or equipment to ope rate without 
any hindrance. 
 
704.3 Stormwater Storage 
1. Stormwater detention is required for all new subdivisions, 
commercial and industrial developments, redevelopment of non -
conforming sites (i.e., existing developed sites that do not have 
detention that have been razed and vacant for greater than six 
months), and other developments that the County deems required 
for protection of downstream properties.

inspect any detention facilities to verify that regular main tenance 
activities are being performed. Final Plats; Covenants, 
Conditions, and Restrictions (CC&R’s); and/or Development 
Plans shall include a special note stating that (1) the owner(s) 
shall be solely responsible for the operation, maintenance, and 
liability for all detention facilities; and (2) the County may 
periodically inspect said detention facilities to verify that regular 
maintenance activities are being performed adequately. 
19. No part of a private detention basin shall be constructed in a public 
right-of-way or public utility easement.

20. Site designs which consolidate detention areas into a limited 
number of larger facilities are preferred over designs which utilize 
many small facilities. Designs which will demand considerable 
maintenance, will be difficult to maintain and access, or utili ze 
numerous small facilities will not be permitted if other alternatives 
are physically possible. 
21. All new subdivisions are required to provide detention for the 
entire subdivision, including the respective one-half of all abutting 
streets to the subdivision. Two or more subdivisions may partner 
to provide a common detention facility. 
 
704.3.1 Detention Facility Design 
Detention facilities which incorporate basins below grade or 
embankments shall be designed and constructed as permanent 
drainage structures which are protected from long term erosion and are 
as maintenance free as possible. Detention basins and related fac ilities 
should be designed to minimize the following typical problems: 
• grass and vegetation maintenance 
• sedimentation control 
• bank deterioration 
• standing water or soggy surfaces 
• mosquito control 
• blockage of outlet structures 
• litter accumulation 
• maintenance of fences and perimeter plantings 
 
No detention shall retain standing water longer than 36 hours unless the 
facility has been designed and constructed as a permanent body of water 
with appropriate health, safety, and water quality measures for such a 
body of water. 
 
Basin inlet and outlet structures may be at or below grade or a 
combination of both. Drainage crossings or culverts shall be provided 
whenever runoff entering or exiting a basin crosses pedestrian paths or 
sidewalks. 
 
Riprap aprons or other energy dissipating measures should be used at 
all inflow points (side slope and basin floor) to reduce velocities and 
discourage sedimentation.

Low flow channels are required on the bottom of basins which serve as 
multi-use areas and are recommended on all basins. Low flow channels 
should be designed with a minimum longitudinal slope of 0.5 percent. 
Concrete lined low flow channels can be designed  with a minimum 
longitudinal slope of 0.2 percent. 
 
If any portion of a detention basin is a retaining wall, design information 
for determining factors of safety against sliding and overturning is 
required. Provisions shall also be incorporated to prevent seepage 
through and under the retaining wall.  
 
Location and Configuration 
In general, open detention facilities located adjacent to streets or 
buildings are discouraged. No portion of a detention basin shall be 
permitted within any public right-of-way or public utility easement. 
 
Curvilinear or irregular shapes are encouraged for open surface basins, 
whenever possible. The designer should vary the shape and side slopes 
of the basin and maximize the linear footage of the perimeter. Curvilinear 
contours at areas immediately adjacent to walls or structures is 
encouraged. 
 
704.3.2 Slope and Depth Criteria 
The following minimum slope and depth criteria are required for multi -
use basins and basins that have unrestricted access: 
1. A maximum of 2:1  (H:V) for protected side slopes and 3:1  (H:V) 
for unprotected side slopes where depths of ponding are less than 
three feet. 
2. A maximum of 4:1 (H:V) for side slopes where depths of ponding 
exceed 3 feet. 
3. Basins greater than 6 feet in depth will require a benched 
configuration with bench widths at least 3 times the height of the 
slope above it with a minimum width of 6 feet. 
4. Basins containing human activity areas shall incorporate access 
slopes of 8:1 (H:V) or flatter (12:1 (H:V) for ADA compliance) into 
the design for ingress and egress. 
 
A minimum freeboard of 0.5-foot above the 100-year high water elevation 
is recommended for all detention facilities. Freeboard may include 
adjacent parking lot areas.

The basin floor should be graded to drain toward the basin outlet. The 
minimum recommended slope is 0.2 percent. A meandering low flow 
channel across the basin bottom is recommended to accommodate 
frequent flows and prevent standing water. 
 
704.3.3 Landscaping and Surface Treatment 
All detention basins shall include appropriate surface treatment and 
erosion control measures including but not limited to landscaping, 
seeding, grass or sod, rock, gravel, or any combination thereof. 
Regardless of basin side slopes, seeding of the basin t o promote 
vegetation shall be considered in the design to prevent rill and gully 
erosion. 
 
Trees, shrubs, and other native vegetation may be used on basin side 
slopes and periphery. Any landscaping placed on the basin floor shall 
not have a density such that it interferes with the stormwater storage 
function of the basin or regular maintenance activities. For basins located 
adjacent to streets, landscaping density shall be increased along the 
street frontage to screen the basin from the street. 
 
Use of decomposed granite or small gradation rock shall be limited to 
basin side slopes of 3H: 1V or flatter and is not recommended for use on 
basin floors, in flow channels, or at the basin inlets and outlets. Use of 
bio-mass filter landscaping treatment on basin floors is encouraged. 
 
Over-excavation will be required to account for any volume displacement 
from landscaping islands, boulders, or rock riprap placement within the 
basin and shall be noted on the Grading & Drainage and Landscape 
Plans. 
 
704.3.4 Outlet Structures 
Due to multi -frequency detention requirements, the design of several 
detention facilities may require the implementation of multi -stage outlet 
structures. These outlet structures must be carefully designed to 
guarantee the complete drainage of the basin and can be in the form of 
drop inlets, culverts, weirs, orifices, or a  combination of these options. 
The utilization of weirs is highly recommended. It is important to note that 
outlet structures that rely on manual operation for proper functioning are 
prohibited.

Outlet structures for detention basins shall be sized based on hydrologic 
reservoir-routing calculations and stage -discharge relationships. Inlet 
control should not always be assumed on detention facility outlet pipes; 
therefore, outlet pipes should be eva luated using the FHWA, HDS -5 
procedures. 
 
Outlet structures shall be constructed such that they are situated directly 
across from the inlet structure(s) and positioned at the greatest distance 
possible. It is important to maximize the distance between outlet 
structures and inflow points in order t o extend flow paths and detention 
times, facilitating the efficient settling of pollutants and sediment. 
 
Metal outlet pipes extending from a basin side slope or embankment are 
prohibited. All outlet structures utilizing solely a pipe/culver as the main 
outlet must have suitable headwalls, end sections, mitered sloped 
concrete protection, etc. 
 
Outlet culverts for detention facilities shall be 12 inches or larger. Orifice 
plates are allowed if they are permanent, tamper -proof, and connected 
to a 12-inch minimum diameter outlet pipe. Outlet structures with orifice 
plates should have a trash rack to prevent clogging. 
 
Incorporate adequate sediment and debris collection measures into the 
basin design to minimize clogging. Outlet structures shall not be 
oversized to account for debris blockage or clogging. Sediment traps 
should also be incorporated into the design of all multi-use detention 
facilities.  
 
Outlet pipes that pose a risk to children, such as those that directly 
connect to a large storm drain system, should be equipped with a 
bar/grate arrangement as per the safety regulations outlined in the 
International Building Code (IBC). This is necessary to ensure that 
children cannot gain access to the outlet opening. 
 
Local scour at culvert outlets and the long-term downstream degradation 
of the facility must be considered in the overall basin design. To mitigate 
erosion, various measures such as energy dissipators, cut -off walls, 
riprap aprons or basins, and rock lined channels should be implemented. 
These measures aim to decrease outlet velocities and enable the flow to

704.3.5 Detention Embankments 
It is recommended that detention facilities be constructed with the 
storage volume located entirely below the natural ground or finished 
grade adjacent to the facility. Use of detention embankments or berms is 
discourage due to the potential for downstream flood hazard in the event 
of failure; however, the following criteria must be incorporated into the 
detention embankment design, at a minimum: 
1. Vegetated embankments shall be less than 20 feet in height and 
shall have side slopes no steeper than 3:1 ( H:V). Embankments 
protected with riprap or other approved erosion control measure 
shall be no steeper than 2:1 (H:V). 
2. A geotechnical engineering study and slope stability analysis is 
required for embankments exceeding 10 -feet in height or for 
embankment slopes exceeding those given above. See the 
Arizona Administrative Code Dam Safety Procedures for 
additional information and criteria. 
3. Top width of the embankment shall be a minimum of 1/2 the height 
of the embankment. 
4. Design of spillways shall also incorporate adequate erosion 
control and energy dissipating measures to ensure the stability of 
the embankment. The use of concrete spillways is preferred. 
5. Seepage through the embankment and internal erosion, 
particularly along the outside of the primary outlet conduit and 
spillway wall, must also be considered in the design of the 
embankment. Soil used for detention embankments should have 
a relatively low p ermeability after placement and shall be 
compacted to a minimum of 95 percent of AASHTO T -99 
maximum density. 
6. No detention facility can be designed to be a jurisdictional dam 
based on ADWR criteria without approval of the County Engineer. 
 
Public detention facilities that include an embankment must have a 
minimum of 1-foot of freeboard above the spillway elevation. The 
spillway elevation should be set equal to or above the 100 -year water 
surface elevation.

704.3.6 Emergency Overflow 
All detention facilities must include measures for emergency overflow in 
case the main outlet structure fails or if there are storm events that 
exceed the design capacity. The overflow system should be designed to 
handle the maximum discharge during a 100 -year peak flow after 
development. The design criteria should ensure the protection of the 
basin and determine the method of discharge. The overflow should be 
conveyed downstream in the same way it would have done under 
predevelopment, historic conditions. 
 
Spillways for detention facilities utilizing embankments should be 
carefully planned to safeguard the embankment side slopes, especially 
on the downstream side. It is recommended that the spillway be located 
to direct the flow around the embankment on or through natural ground, 
rather than situating the spillway directly above the main outlet structure. 
The safety of individuals, properties downstream, and the potential 
outcomes of embankment failure must be taken into account and 
assessed. 
 
704.3.7 Safety 
Detention facilities in general should be open, visible, and accessible so 
that persons can appreciate any hazard and guard themselves, and so 
that rescue efforts, if necessary, are not impeded. 
 
To reduce the potential dangers associated with detention facilities the 
following recommendations are made in the design and construction: 
1. The ground surface side slopes around the facility should be 
made rough. 
2. Break up ponding water with islands, boulders and mounds; put 
solid objects for holding onto in the ponding area such as large 
plants or rocks. 
3. Avoid sudden constrictions and high velocities at outlets. Broad 
open rectangular weirs are preferable to anything involving the 
mouths of pipes and/or creating a hazardous vortex at the outlet. 
4. Restricting public access and/or identifying potential hazards 
associated with detention basins, particularly in multi-use areas. 
 
If detention facilities must be designed with steeper side slopes or 
vertical walls, adequate routes out of the basin should be provided.

Signage should be provided to inform the public of the basin purpose and 
potential safety hazard from stormwater. (e.g., DANGER - This basin is 
designed to collect stormwater runoff DO NOT ENTER during rainy or 
threatening weather). 
 
704.3.8 Security Barriers 
Detention basins that adhere to the Slope and Depth Criteria Section and 
the preceding sections should eliminate the need for security barriers to 
prevent unauthorized access. However, it is recommended to install 
security barriers, equipped with maintenance access gates, along the top 
of basin side slopes steeper than 3:1  (H:V) and in areas where water 
depths exceed 3 feet. 
 
These security barriers can be constructed using materials such as 
masonry, chain-link, or wrought-iron (pool-type) fencing, and must have 
a minimum height of 72 inches. It is important to ensure that the fencing, 
if required, does not impede the hydraulic  capacity of the inlet or outlet 
structures. 
 
For retaining walls or inlet/outlet structure headwalls and wingwalls that 
are over 30 inches in height, appropriate safety railings are required. 
Show detailed sections of the proposed barriers on the grading and 
drainage plans or development plans, as applicable. 
 
705 Building in a Flood Zone 
Constructing in flood zones necessitates thorough due diligence, 
particularly in terms of foundation type, base flood elevation (BFE), 
frequency of flood events, ceiling height, and the financial implications of 
National Flood Insurance  Program (NFIP). The base flood elevation 
(BFE) denotes the elevation linked to a one percent probability of an 
annual flood occurrence. 
 
Flood zones are geographic areas that FEMA has defined according to 
levels of flood risk.

Table 705.1 Flood Zones and Risk 
 
705.1 Floodplain Management Regulations 
The County is responsible for adopting and enforcing floodplain 
management regulations so that development, including the construction 
of buildings are undertaken in a way that reduces exposure to flooding. 
 
The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) requires the County to 
agree to do all of the following: 
• Adopt and enforce flood maps as well as flood damage prevention 
ordinance 
• Require permits for development in a floodplain 
• Assure building sites are reasonably safe from flooding 
• Establish base flood elevations (BFE) where not determined by 
FEMA 
• Require new and substantially improved home and manufactured 
home to be elevated above the BFE 
• Require non-residential buildings to be elevated above the BFE 
or dry floodproofed 
• Determine if damaged building is substantially damaged 
• Conduct field inspections to cite and remedy violations 
• Require and maintain surveyed elevation information to document 
compliance 
• Carefully consider requests for variances 
• Resolve non-compliance and violations

705.2 National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) 
An elevation certification is required to obtain an insurance quote. 
 
705.3 Removing Property from a Flood Zone 
FEMA approvals take considerable time, typically 60- to 90-days due to 
respond and rush processing is not an option. DO NOT commence 
building before FEMA issues a finding. The following steps are required 
to remove a property from a flood zone. 
 
To request removing a property from a flood zone, it must be proven that 
the: 
1. property will not suffer flood damage 
2. property higher than 100-year BFE  
 
The property must be removed from the floodplain before building to 
avoid the requirement to acquire flood insurance. 
 
The removal process with FEMA typically requires the services of a civil 
engineer and/or surveyor. The land surveyor will determine if the existing 
ground is above or below the BFE. 
 
705.3.1 Natural Grade is above the BFE 
If the natural ground is above the BFE and no fill is required to raise the 
grade above the BFE, then a Letter of Map Amendment (LOMA) is 
required. 
 
705.3.2 Fill is Required to Raise Grade above the BFE 
Prior to placing any fill on the site: 
• Obtain a County floodplain permit for the placement of fill in the 
floodplain 
• A grading plan is required showing existing elevations, proposed 
finished grade that is above the current BFE 
 
The County will review the permit and determine if revisions are required, 
such as additional fill to placed elsewhere onsite to offset the fill placed

800 General Information 
The intent of this Chapter is to establish guidelines and criteria for Traffic 
Engineering design and construction in the County . The minimum 
requirements outlined in this Chapter are focused on ensuring safet y. 
Therefore, standards that offer a higher level of safety should be used. 
 
801 Traffic Signals 
The County does not  own, maintain or install  traffic signals.  Any 
development plans that involve signalization must be coordinated with the 
County and the maintenance shall be the responsibility of th e developer, 
HOA, or property owners. Refer to ADOT Traffic Guidelines and 
Processes for the necessary requirements and standards for conducting 
a Traffic Signal Study. 
 
Traffic signals shall conform to ADOT Specifications and Drawings, 
unless otherwise approved by the County. 
 
802 Street Lighting 
The County does not own, install, or maintain streetlights. Developers are 
responsible for coordinating any plans for street lighting with the County 
and assume maintenance responsibilities themselves, or through an 
HOA, or property owner(s), or by forming a lighting improvement district. 
 
Designers should review the County’s Outdoor Lighting Ordinance 02-88 
(1998) and ADOT Traffic Guidelines and Processes  for roadway 
illumination requirements and guidance. 
 
Street lighting shall conform to ADOT Specifications and Drawings, 
unless otherwise approved by the County.

803 Pavement Marking and Signing 
All required pavement markings, traffic control devices, and road name 
signs for new and/or existing roads must be shown on the plans and shall 
be installed and paid for by the developer. 
 
The pavement markings, signing and sign supports shall conform to 
ADOT Standard Specifications and Details, including but not limited to the 
following: 
• FHWA Manual of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) 
• ADOT Supplement to the MUTCD 
• ADOT Manual of Approved Signs (MOAS) 
• ADOT Signing and Marking Standard (SMS) Drawings 
• ADOT Standard Specifications 
• ADOT Traffic Guidelines and Processes 
 
Signs shall be installed on breakaway supports for roads with a design 
speed of 50 mph or higher. Whenever a sign is replaced or upgraded, the 
support must also meet breakaway compliance, subject to available 
funding. 
 
In subdivision development with stub roads, signs shall be installed at the 
end of the stub roads and indicated that the road will be extended in the 
future. The sign shall have a message stating: “This Road is to be 
extended with Future Development. For More Information Contact the 
Navajo County Planning & Development Ser vices.” The developer is 
responsible for providing this sign which shall be made of a 0.080 -in. 
gauge aluminum sign blank and fully reflective (minimum engineering 
grade material) sheeting and designed per the MUTCD.

804 Traffic Control 
Projects and public functions in County right -of-way require a traffic 
control plan review and approval from the County. Traffic control plans 
shall conform to the following guidelines: 
1. The safety of the public and construction personnel takes 
precedence over all other considerations. 
2. Provision for access by emergency response vehicles must be in 
place at all times. 
3. Access to adjoining properties must be available at all times. 
4. Schools, hospitals, and other public service organizations must be 
made aware of the project and level and duration of impact prior to 
starting construction. Notification shall be the responsibility of the 
permittee. 
5. Traffic control shall utilize and conform to the following documents: 
• Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) 
• ADOT Temporary Traffic Control Design Guidelines 
• ADOT Supplement to the MUTCD 
• ADOT Manual of Approved Signs (MOAS) 
• ADOT Standard Specifications 
• ADOT Traffic Guidelines and Processes

900 Grading and Sediment Control 
It is crucial to take into account  various factors such as conserving the 
natural environmental function of the site, ensuring compatibility with the 
surrounding land, stabilizing hillsides and slopes prone to erosion, 
preserving drainage courses, and protecting natural drainage ways when 
planning and implementing grading activities. 
 
900.1 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose of this Chapter is to prevent loss of life and property by 
regulating development, safeguarding watersheds and natural 
waterways, eliminating adverse drainage conditions in new 
developments, preventing soil erosion, reducing land disturbance, 
promoting preservation of land's natural character and aesthetic value, 
maintaining the visual appeal of graded sites, and preserving the existing 
landscape by retaining natural topographic features, native vegetation, 
and wildlife habitat. 
 
900.2 County Code, Ordinances and Standards 
Excavation and grading activities shall comply with the regulations and 
ordinances set forth in this Manual. 
 
All earthwork, clearing and grubbing, and other site preparation work shall 
conform to the requirements of the International Building Code  (for 
buildings and site improvements), MAG Specifications or ADOT 
Specification (for roads), and this Manual, unless otherwise specified in 
the approved geotechnical report. In the event of any inconsistencies 
between the International Building Code , MAG Specifications,  or the 
requirements in this Manual, the more rigorous of the two will be enforced. 
 
The design of drainage systems must meet the standards outlined in 
Chapter 700 of this Manual. In the event of any discrepancies between 
Chapter 700 and other sections, the requirements of Chapter 700 will 
prevail. 
 
901 Permits 
A County grading permit must be obtained before any grading is done, 
unless exempted in this Chapter. Each site requires a separate permit, 
which can cover both excavations and fills.

Engaging in or allowing any clearing or grading activities on a site is strictly 
prohibited, unless a permit is obtained. The only exception to this rule is 
conducting soil tests on a piece of land that is no larger than 100 square 
feet. Whether it is vacant lots or developed lots in non-disturbance areas 
in all zoning districts, any clearing or grading requires a grading permit 
and prior approval from the County. It is important to note that no clearing 
or grading should exceed a defensible space, which is  a strip of land 
extending up to a maximum of 30 feet horizontally from any structure. 
Removing any cacti, shrub, or plant within the defensible space is only 
allowed if it has been confirmed as dead by the County. 
 
The removal of dead trees within the designated defensible area is 
required. Vegetation under trees should be maintained at a height that 
prevents a fire from spreading easily. Proper maintenance of l ive 
vegetation in the defensible area is required to minimize  intensity and 
spread of fires. Vacant lot owners must follow the recommendations for 
establishing a defensible space from neighboring structures. Without 
written authorization from the County, clearing for a defensible space in 
undisturbed areas is prohibited. Clearing of vacant lots is only allowed for 
the purpose of creating a defensible space near a structure. It is forbidden 
to eliminate wildlife habitat for protected species. 
 
No work shall commence within a floodplain without prior consultation with 
the County and an issuance of a permit. See Chapter 700. 
 
901.1 Requirements 
To acquire a Grading Permit, all of the following criteria must be satisfied: 
1. The application for a grading permit shall include submittal items 
as outlined in Chapter 200 of this Manual. Plans shall be drawn to 
scale and shall be per the County’s CADD Standards and be of 
sufficient clarity to indicate the nature and extent of the work 
proposed and show in detail that they will conform to the provisions 
in this Manual and al l relevant laws, ordinances, rules and 
regulations. 
2. Grading Plans shall be prepared by a Professional Engineer and at 
a minimum shall include the following: 
a. Location of the work, the name and address of the 
owner, and the person by whom they were prepared.

901.2 Issuance 
The regulations outlined this Manual are relevant to grading permits. In 
the event of unforeseen delays arising from factors that were not taken 
into account during the issuance of the permit, the County has the

901.3 Exemptions 
1. Single Family Residential where the excavation is: 
a. Less than 50 cubic yards, 
b. Less than 2 feet in depth and 
c. Does not create a cut slope 5 feet or greater in height and 
steeper than 1.5:1 (H:V). 
2. When approved by the County, grading in an isolated, self -
contained area if there is no impact or danger to private or public 
property. 
3. An excavation below finished grade for basements and footings of 
a building, retaining wall, or other structure authorized by a valid 
building permit. This shall not exempt any fill made with the material 
from such excavation or exempt any excavation havin g an 
unsupported height greater than 5 feet after the completion of such 
structure. 
4. Cemetery graves. 
5. Refuse disposal sites controlled by other regulations. 
6. Excavations for wells, tunnels, or utilities. 
7. Mining, quarrying, excavating, processing, or stockpiling of rock, 
sand, grave, aggregate or clay where established and provided for 
by law, provided such operations do not affect the lateral support 
or increase the stresses in or pressure upon any adjacen t or 
contiguous property. 
8. Exploratory excavations under the direction of soil engineers or 
geologists. 
9. A fill that meets the following criteria: 
a. not intended to support structures, and 
b. does not exceed 50-cubic yards (38.3-cubic meters) on any 
one lot, and 
c. does not obstruct a drainage course, and 
d. is either: 
i. less than 1 foot in depth and placed on natural terrain 
with a slope flatter than 5:1 (H:V or 20 percent slope), 
or 
ii. less than 3 feet in depth 
 
An exemption from the permit requirements does not imply authorization 
for any work to be carried out in a manner that violates the provisions of 
this Chapter or any other laws or ordinances of this jurisdiction.

902 Standards and Design Criteria 
 
902.1 At-Risk Grading 
Before accepting an At -Risk Grading and Drainage plan for County 
review, the County must conduct an initial review of the project’s Grading 
and Drainage plan. All significant County comments on the Grading and 
Drainage plan must be resolved before accepting the At-Risk Grading and 
Drainage plan. While an At-Risk Grading and Drainage Plan approval may 
be granted for the developer’s convenience, it is important to note that the 
County is not obligated to approve an At-Risk Rough Grading Plan. If there 
is a lack of timely progress towards the final approval of the Grading and 
Drainage plan, the permit may be revoked. 
 
At-Risk Grading and Drainage plans are solely approved for rough grading 
purposes. Trenching or fine grading is not permitted under the At -Risk 
Grading and Drainage plan approval. 
 
The Professional Engineer shall work  to finalize the approval of the 
complete Grading and Drainage plan while the At -Risk Grading and 
Drainage plans are being utilized, as failure to do so may result in the 
revocation of the At-Risk Grading and Drainage permit. 
 
902.2 Pre-Grading 
A grading or building permit shall not be contingent upon altering, 
modifying, or not utilizing existing grading, provided that the existing 
grading work has a valid permit and does not pose a risk to the proposed 
development or neighboring properties. This clause does not prohibit the 
County from requiring documentation to verify site suitability for soil 
stability, compaction, and other geotechnical considerations. 
 
902.3 Clearing and Grubbing 
Clearing and grubbing is work performed in advance of grading operations 
to remove vegetation, rubbish, debris and other objectional material from 
the right-of-way, easement, and such other areas. 
 
Perform clearing and grubbing in accordance with MAG Specifications 
Section 201.

902.4 Benching 
 
902.4.1 Fill Slopes 
When constructing new embankments on existing embankments, fill 
slopes, or hillsides, benching (Figure 902.1) shall be required to key-in the 
new embankment to minimize the possibility of slippage at the interface. 
A determination of the need for benching at each location shall be made 
by the designer and geotechnical engineer. Show benching details and 
locations on the plans.  
 
Figure 902.1 Typical Fill Slope Benching 
 
902.4.2 Cut Slopes 
Benching of new cut slopes is a special design and is to be investigated 
and designed individually for each cut area where benching of the new cut 
slope is being considered. A geotechnical report is required and must 
include benching details and requirements. 
 
902.4.3 Mini-Benching 
Mini-Benching is a special slope treatment used to promote re-vegetation, 
reduce erosion. See ADOT Roadside Development Section's 
Erosion/Sediment Best Management Practices and Details.

902.5 Excavations and Cuts 
The slope of cut surfaces shall not exceed what is deemed safe for the 
designated purposed and shall not exceed a ratio of 2:1 (H:V). Steeper 
cut slopes may be considered when a  sealed geotechnical report is 
provided by the permit holder. The geotechnical report must confirm that 
the area has been thoroughly investigated and the Geotechnical Engineer 
gives an opinion that a steeper cut slope will not pose a risk to public or 
private property. 
 
Excavations and cuts shall comply with MAG Specifications Section 205. 
The County has the authority to require the use of ADOT Specification  
Section 203.  
 
902.5.1 Surplus Material 
Prior to the exportation of any material from a site, a suitable location for 
the material must be identified in order to obtain a grading permit for its 
removal. Surplus material can only be exported to the approved site 
specified on the approved grading plans. Alternate receiving sites shall 
only be used after grading plan is revised, resubmitted to the County, and 
the amended is approved. 
 
902.5.2 Structure Excavation and Structure Backfill 
Structure excavation and structure backfill shall comply with MAG 
Specifications Section 206. The County has the authority to require the 
use of ADOT Specification Section 203. 
 
902.5.3 Borrow Excavation 
Borrow excavation is the excavation of material required for construction 
embankments or fills from on -site locations. Borrow excavations shall 
comply with MAG Specifications Section 210. The County has the 
authority to require the use of ADOT Specification Section 203.  
 
902.6 Embankments and Fill Construction 
All fills and berms shall not exceed a height of 8 feet, measured from the 
highest nearby natural grade to the top of the fill, unless authorized by the 
County. All fills within setback limits shall not exceed a height of 4 feet. 
The placement of embankmen ts shall comply with MAG Specifications 
Section 211. The County has the authority to require the use of ADOT 
Specification Section 203.

902.6.1 Importation of Fill Material 
Except as exempted in the International Building Code the importation of 
fill material is prohibited unless a grading permit allowing such is first 
secured. 
 
902.6.2 Geotechnical Investigation 
A geotechnical investigation is required for all projects that include 
roadways; major structures in the right -of-way, such as bridges or box 
culverts; underground facility design, including storm drain, water, and 
sewer; or when natural slopes are steeper than 4:1 (H:V). 
 
902.6.3 Placement of Fill 
Organic matter is prohibited in fills unless a sealed engineering report is 
submitted and approved by the County. Rocks or other non -reducible 
materials larger than 12  inches in size are not permitted in fills, unless 
specifically approved by the County. If larger rocks are permitted, a 
geotechnical Professional Engineer must inspect and approve the 
placement and stability of the fill. 
 
902.6.4 Slopes and Benching 
Fill slopes shall be no steeper than is safe for the intended use and shall 
be no steeper than 3 :1 (H:V), unless otherwise approved in the 
geotechnical report. 
 
Benching shall be as required by the International Building Code and as 
determined by the geotechnical and design engineer. 
 
902.6.5 Compaction 
All fills shall be compacted per the Table 902.1 and ADOT Specifications. 
 
Table 902.1 Fill Compaction

Open Space 90% 
Roadways, Driveways, Parking Lots 95% 
Structures or Building Pads Per Geotechnical Report 
* Unless otherwise indicated in a sealed and approved geotechnical report.

902.6.6 Blending of Fill Grading 
Fill grading should have an irregular and contoured edge that blends into 
the natural surrounding terrain. 
902.7 Setbacks 
Setback dimensions and cut/fill slope requirements shall be in accordance 
with International Building Code. In cases where a fill slope is situated 
close to the site boundary, additional measures may be required by the 
County to safeguard neighboring prope rties from potential damage 
caused by grading activities. These precautions may include but are not 
limited to: 
• Additional setbacks 
• Provision for retaining or slough walls 
• Mechanical or chemical treatment of the fill slope surface to 
minimize erosion 
• Provisions for the control of surface waters 
 
The County has the authority to grant alternative setback approvals. The 
County may require an investigation and recommendation from a licensed 
Professional Engineer or geologist to verify compliance with the 
requirements outlined in this section. 
 
902.8 Grading for Parks and Golf Courses 
The County has the authority to waive the restrictions on disturbance, 
such as disturbed areas and the height and retention of cuts and fills, for 
the purpose of developing a park, a golf course, trails, or any other 
recreational facility that does not involve constructing buildings as its main 
objective. 
 
903 Hillside Disturbance Standards 
The hillside standards aim to limit the amount  of hillside disturbance on 
each property based on slope severity. Hillside areas are defined as those 
with slopes equal to or greater than 20 percent, as indicated on a 
topographical contour map prepared by an Arizona -registered land 
surveyor. Slope percentage is determined by contour line spacing on the 
preliminary plat.  The County requires the submission of topographic 
contour maps with specific requirements based on Table 903.1.

903.1 Exemption - Calculations 
Unless otherwise stated in this Manual, all disturbance activities are 
subject to regulation. If permitted, any exempted disturbance activities will 
be deducted from the total area of the property. The "Preservation 
Requirement" and "Disturbance Allowance"  areas, as mentioned earlier, 
will be calculated based on the remaining net area of the property after 
subtracting the exempted disturbance areas from the total area of 
development.

the development of utility lines and associated equipment, outside 
of any disturbance caused by other development activities, either 
pre-existing or current, may be exempted from the requirements of 
this section upon administrative review by and approval of a "Utility 
Disturbance Permit" by the County. Utility Disturbance Permits 
shall only be issued in conformance with the Following conditions.

903.2 Specified Nonexempt Activities 
The Hillside Disturbance Standards do not exemption to the following

1. Disturbance activities for the development of any effluent watering 
field or any lake or pond intended for the storage of treated effluent, 
or any service and/or access road or any above or below ground 
pipeline or utility lines, whether or not the develop ment of such 
fields, ponds, lakes, service/access roads, pipelines or utility lines 
have been mandated or suggested by another governmental 
agency or Court. 
2. Any "utility" disturbance, other than for a utility line and associated 
equipment as described in Section 903.1.1. 
3. In addition to the detailed information that is required to be provided 
to the County to ensure compliance with this Manual and 
Ordinances, the property owner may submit to the County an

construction on the property. 
 
903.3 Previously Disturbed Areas 
Hillside areas that have been previously disturbed within a development 
will be included in the overall hillside disturbance calculation for the 
development and will not be considered as undisturbed hillside areas by 
the County. If an applicant wishes to salvage landscape materials for re -
vegetation before Final Plat approval, they may do so,  but at the risk of 
not complying with this Standard and having the final plat denied. 
 
903.4 Determination of Natural Grade.  
The topography of land in the County as of January 1, 2025, is considered 
to be natural grade by this Standard. Any grading or disturbance activities 
carried out after January 1, 2025 , will not be exempt from the Hillside 
Disturbance Standards, and any cumulative hillside disturbance shall be 
offset at the time of development approval in accordance with the Hillside 
Protection Standards. 
 
903.5 Disturbance Buffers and Fencing 
 
903.5.1 Fencing 
With the exception of Section 903.5.2, once a disturbance area is defined, 
an area that meets the hillside protection requirements of the lot, parcel, 
or tract must be safeguarded by using rope and flag, which should be 
securely fixed in the ground to prevent any movement. The roped-in area 
should encompass all previously disturbed areas as well as any areas that

of undisturbed areas or hillside protection areas disturbed prior to 
January 1, 2025, if it is in line with an approved landscape plan. The rope 
and flags shall only be removed once all construction activities on the lot 
have been completed. 
 
903.5.2 No Fencing 
If the County deems fencing requirements impracticable, they may waive 
such requirements at their discretion. In such cases, the designated area 
to be disturbed must include a perimeter area that is at least 20 feet wide 
around all other construction or gr ading activities. The proposed 
disturbance perimeter, as indicated on approved grading plans, must be 
iron-staked by an Arizona -registered land surveyor or civil engineer, 
roped, and have warning signs posted prior to any disturbance activities. 
The County must inspect the staking, roping, and warning signage prior 
to any disturbance activity occurs. These markers must remain in place 
throughout construction and can only be removed after final approval is 
granted by the County, or in the case of a multifamily development, after 
a Certificate of Occupancy is issued. 
 
903.6 Utility Disturbance 
Excavation work for utility line installation, such as water, septic systems, 
sewer mains, and laterals, must be confined to a designated area 
centered on the utility line, with a width that may vary depending on the 
requirements of the work. Any activitie s outside of this designated area 
are prohibited. 
 
903.7 Subdivider Options 
To comply with the Hillside Disturbance Standards, the developer of a 
property where future disturbance activities are planned may select one 
of two options. 
 
903.7.1 Lot-by-Lot Hillside Protection Option 
If the developer chooses not to use the Hillside Transfer and Protection 
Option outlined in Section 903.7.2 to comply with these Standards, and if 
no hillside protection measures are proposed (apart from those required 
in Section 903.3) during the platting process for the undisturbed but 
developable lots or parcels within site, then each lot or parcel must

903.7.2 Hillside Transfer and Protection Option 
1. If the developer opts to transfer allowable hillside disturbance from 
undisturbed hillside areas to lots, parcels, tracts or rights -of-way 
within a development, they may do so by identifying an area 
approved by the County and granting to the County a Hills ide 
Protection Easement(s) to the County. In case the Hillside Transfer 
and Protection Option is used, all areas outside of the Hillside 
Protection Easement(s) in the development may be disturbed 
through the subdivision improvement process and/or future 
development activities. 
2. In the event that the developer selects the Hillside Transfer and 
Protection Option to preserve the required amount of hillside areas 
within the development, the following regulations apply: 
a. If a development spans two or more zoning districts, the 
amount of hillside slopes to be preserved in each zoning 
district will be calculated separately. 
b. The total required undisturbed hillside areas for the

development. Hillside Protection Easements can be placed

903.8 Clearance for Fire Safety 
The Fire Marshal has the authority to inspect and approve limited clearing 
and removal of plant material within a non-disturbance area on the lot for 
up to 100 feet from a structure in order to mitigate fire hazards caused by 
excessive growth and the buildup of dead or dying plant material. The 
purpose of this is to minimize fire risks by requiring the removal of 
materials that pose a fire hazard. No replanting is permitted within the non-
disturbance areas under this Section. Any activities exceeding the Fire 
Marshal’s authorization will constitute a violation and may incur relevant 
fines and fees.  
 
903.9 Enforcement - Remediation 
If disturbance activities are found to be in violation of this Section, the 
Planning & Development Services Director or their designee is authorized 
to enforce these regulations. This includes, but is not limited to, the ability 
to mandate the immediate installation of chain -link fencing around all 
disturbance perimeters, the immediate re -vegetation of any illegally 
disturbed areas, and the issuance of project-wide stop work orders. 
 
904 Hillside Local Streets 
In hillside areas where the existing slopes exceed 15 percent, it is possible 
to use hillside local street standards to promote a more suitable adaptation 
to the area's topography. If there are notable topographical elements like 
washes, hillsides, boulders, rock outcroppings, and established native 
vegetation that cannot be restored, alt ernative engineering designs may 
be approved. These modifications will be evaluated on a case -by-case 
basis and require approval from the County. The subsequent section 
outlines the prerequisites and design options for constructing local streets 
in hillside areas. 
 
904.1 Grading Disturbance 
The grading process for both public and private streets must adhere to the 
to this Manual, including the limitations on cut and fill activities as well as 
land disturbance. Any disturbance caused by road grading will decrease 
the overall allowance for hillside disturbance across the entire 
development, as specified in this Chapter. If road grading results in 
disturbance outside of street right-of-way or private road street tracts that

904.2 Revegetation 
The developer must ensure that re -vegetation and restoration take place 
in areas where scarring occurs due to street or utility construction. These 
restored areas shall be carefully graded and landscaped to blend in with 
the surrounding natural vegetation and terrain. Additionally, measures 
must be taken to stabilize these areas to prevent erosion. It is important 
that landscaping and stabilization activities are carried out simultaneously 
with the construction process. 
 
Disturbed Forest Service land requires an approved US Forest Service 
(USFS) revegetation plan and seeding design. 
 
905 Washes and Drainage 
 
905.1 Maintenance of Continuity 
Designers, developers, and contractors shall preserve of the entry and 
exit points and the uninterrupted flow of all natural drainage channels on 
lot or parcel. The ponding of water above cut or fill slopes is  prohibited. 
Design building sites  to divert surface waters away from structures and 
retaining walls. 
 
905.2 Swale Grading 
Swale grading for drainage needs is exempt from the restoration 
procedures. 
 
905.3 Character 
Enhance the appearance of retained washes and new drainage channels 
to blend in seamlessly with the surrounding environment. Utilize rock and 
native plant materials in landscaping efforts, while also prioritizing the 
conservation of existing natural elements. 
 
905.4 Detention Basins 
Stormwater detention basins utilizing natural materials are recommended, 
pending approval from the County Engineer based on specific conditions 
and locations.

905.5 Detention Basin Re-vegetation/Aesthetics 
Stormwater detention basins shall be re -vegetated using the existing 
vegetation and native plant materials, as deemed appropriate based on 
the approved landscape plan. The implementation of terracing, berming, 
and contouring techniques are encouraged to enhance the naturalization 
and visual appeal of the basin, ensuring it seamlessly integrates with the 
surrounding terrain. 
 
905.6 Basin Construction 
Design basins to facilitate the formation of peninsulas, enhance the 
“natural” contouring, and strategically position boulders and rock 
outcroppings. 
 
905.7 Basin Slopes 
Basin slopes shall not exceed a 3:1 (H:V) slope. The County may approve 
deviations from this requirement if a lesser slope would result in excessive 
grading of the existing environment. 
 
905.8 Native Materials 
The use of native materials in the construction of headwalls, flow retardant 
structures and devices, culverts and drainage channel bottoms is 
encouraged. 
 
905.9 Erosion Prevention 
See Section 907. 
 
906 Retaining Walls 
The County requires a permit and a sealed engineering design for 
masonry and concrete retaining walls for the following conditions: 
• Retaining walls exceeding a height of (4) feet 
• Retaining walls below four (4) feet in height, but meeting one of the 
following conditions: 
o Surcharge loading from structures or vehicles 
o Having a backslope exceeding 10:1 (H:V) within a distance 
equal to the retaining wall’s height, or ten (10) feet, 
whichever is greater. 
o Horizontal spacing between terraced walls is less than two 
(2) times the height of the taller wall.

Before the County will close a wall permit, the applicant is required to 
obtain final inspection and approval from the engineer who is responsible

ADOT Structure Detail Drawings (SD-Std) may be used . Retaining walls 
used in conjunction with or adjacent to stormwater conveyance or 
detention facilities, and subject to inundation or flow, shall be specifically 
designed to withstand these conditions. 
 
906.1 Terraced Walls 
Terraced retaining walls are subject to the retaining wall height limitations. 
In cases where two retaining walls are separated by a landscaped terrace 
that is at least as wide as the height of the taller wall, each wall will be 
treated as an individual wa ll. The distance between terraced retaining 
walls is measured from wall face to wall face. 
 
906.2 Determination of Average Height 
The height of a retaining wall is measured from the top of footing to the 
top of wall. The length of a retaining wall is measured along the lay out 
line of the wall as defined on the plans or details and includes any straight 
or curved sections. The average height is then determined by calculating 
the total vertical surface area of the wall, as noted above, then dividing 
the total vertical surface area by the wall’s total length. 
 
906.3 Height Limitations 
The maximum allowable height and average height of a retaining wall, 
including straight-line or circular sections of a meandering wall, shall not 
exceed the following: 
 
Table 906.1 Wall Height Limitations 
 
Average Slope at Wall* 0% – 15% > 15% 
Maximum Height 8 feet 10 feet 
Average Height 6 feet 7 feet 
* As determined by averaging percentage of slopes shown on sections 
through grading plan submittal.

906.4 Stacked Rock and Mechanically Stabilized Earth 
Retaining Walls 
Design stacked stone and Mechanically Stabilized Earth (MSE) retaining 
walls for non -roadway applications in accordance with the guidelines 
provided by the National Concrete Masonry Association (NCMA) Design 
Manual for Segmental Retaining Walls. 
 
907 Erosion Control 
Construct and maintain e rosion controls to prevent erosion of all slopes 
and graded areas. Provide surface drainage interceptors at the top of all 
cut and fill slopes where surface runoff will create erosion problems. Install 
sub-surface drainage facilities stability and protection of affected areas 
due to ground water seepage. Erosion protection of drainage swales is 
encouraged using native rocks and native plant materials. Where runoff 
velocities necessitate additional erosion protection, the use of integ ral 
colored gunite or alternative material may be approved by the County. 
 
Erosion control measures and best management practices shall be in 
accordance with ADOT Roadside Development standards and details. 
 
907.1 Construction Phase Erosion Control 
Install erosion control measures during construction as soon as 
practicable and prior to the forecast that rain is imminent. See  Chapter 
700. 
 
907.1.1 Permanent Erosion Control 
The faces of cut and fill slopes shall be prepared and maintained to 
prevent erosion. Slope stabilization is required for all grading work 
involving cut and fill slopes that are two (2) feet or higher. Protective 
measures may not be necessary where cut slo pes are considered 
erosion-resistant, such as in situ granite. Options for slope stabilization 
include: 
• Re-vegetated banks with a mix of reseeding/seed mats, trees, 
shrubs, groundcover, rock, and riprap. Plant type, size and 
coverage shall be sufficient to stabilize and begin restoring. 
• For manufactured banks higher than 8 feet, a natural appearance 
should be created (such as a combination of rough-cut, undulating, 
and/or rounded toe and top of slope), with terracing improve plant 
establishment.

908 Grading Inspection 
Grading activities that fall within the scope of a grading permit shall be 
inspected and tested. The responsibility of arranging and covering the 
costs of these inspections lies with the owner, who must hire a civil 
Professional Engineer, geotechnical Professional Engineer, or geologist. 
Before the work can be accepted, the County requires submission of 
testing results and reports documenting the grading activities. 
 
908.1 Pad Elevation and Building Location Certifications  
Before a building stem wall inspection or pre-slab inspection is approved, 
the property owner or their representative must submit a certification 
statement to the County. This statement shall be prepared, stamped, and 
signed by an Arizona -registered land surveyor, confirming the finished 
floor elevation(s) and the horizontal location of the building. The accuracy 
of pad elevations and building locations must be within 1/10th of a foot in 
comparison to the approved site plan or any amended site plan. The 
County Engi neer may choose to waive these requirements if deemed 
appropriate. 
 
908.2 Permittee 
The permittee is responsible for the performed work in accordance with 
the approved plans and specifications, as well as in conformance to the 
provisions of the building codes. The permittee must engage consultants, 
as necessary, to provide professional in spections on a timely basis. The 
permittee shall act as a coordinator between the consultants, the 
contractor, and the County. In the event of changed conditions, the 
permittee is responsible for notifying the County and submitting revised 
plans for approval.

908.3 Civil Engineer 
The civil engineer is responsible for conducting comprehensive 
inspections within their specific area of expertise. These inspections 
include observing and reviewing the establishment of line, grade, and 
surface drainage of the site. In modifications are n ecessary, the civil 
engineer will develop updated plans and seek County approval. 
 
908.4 Geotechnical Engineer 
The geotechnical engineer is responsible for conducting inspections 
within their specific area of expertise. These inspections shall include 
closely monitoring the grading process and conducting tests to ensure the 
required fill materials quality and compa ction are achieved. The 
geotechnical engineer must also carefully observe the preparation of the 
subgrade, as well as the placement and compaction of the fill, to ensure 
that the work is carried out in accordance with the approved plan and the 
relevant regulations outline in this Manual. If any conditions deviate from 
the approved geotechnical report, the engineer must submit revised plans 
and reports to the County for approval. 
 
908.5 Geologist 
The geologist is responsible for conducting a thorough inspection within 
their specific area of technical expertise. These inspections shall include 
observing the excavation of the bedrock to assess whether the conditions 
and grading activities align with the approved geotechnical report. If any 
conditions are found to deviate from the approved geotechnical report, the 
geologist must submit revised plans and reports to the County for 
approval.  
 
908.6 County 
The County is responsible for conducting inspections throughout the 
project’s different phases to ensure compliance with the project plans, 
reports and specifications. The permittee must furnish the County with 
copies of testing and inspections reports per formed by an engineer or 
geologist.  
 
908.7 Noncompliance 
If the event that the civil engineer, geotechnical engineer, or geologist 
determines that the work is not in compliance with the requirements 
outlined in this Chapter or the approved grading plans, they must

If there is a change in the designated civil engineer, geotechnical

909 Completion of Work 
Upon completion of the rough grading work and the final completion of the 
work, the following reports, drawings, and supplements are required, as 
applicable: 
1. A Record Drawing, as outlined in Chapter 300 of this Manual and 
the Record Drawings Checklist. 
2. A comprehensive report prepared by the geotechnical engineer 
hired to provide their services. This report shall include the 
locations and elevations of field density tests, summaries of both 
field and laboratory tests, supporting data, and comments on any 
modifications made during the grading process and their impact on 
the recommendations stated in the approved geotechnical report. 
The geotechnical engineer shall submit a statement confirming 
that, to the best of their knowledge, the work within their area  of 
responsibility adheres to the approved geotechnical report and 
relevant provisions of this Manual. 
3. If required by the grading permit, a report prepared by the geologist 
who was retained to provide their expertise. This report shall 
include a final description of the site’s geology and any new 
information discovered during the grading process, along with  its 
impacts on the recommendations shown on the approved grading 
plan. The geologist shall submit a statement affirming that, to the 
best of their knowledge, the work within their area of responsibility 
complies with the approved geology report and relevant provisions 
of this Manual. 
4. The grading contractor shall submit a statement of conformance to 
the approved grading plans, using a form provided by the County.

1000 General Information 
The purpose of this Chapter is to establish landscaping standards and 
guidelines within County Right-of-Way. These guidelines aim to maintain 
and enhance the environmental qualities of the County , mitigate the 
impacts of adjacent uses, and improve the quality and appearance of new 
or existing development.  
 
Landscaping within the Right -of-Way may be permitted  as long as it 
complies with the AASHTO Roadside Design Guide . It shall not obstruct 
sight distance, cause visibility issues, pose safety hazards, or damage 
road, drainage or utility infrastructure. If landscaping is placed in roadside 
drainage channel or on side -slopes, the materials shall not impede the 
drainage flow or reduce the channel’s cross-sectional area. 
 
Environmentally compatible landscaping plays a crucial role in enhancing 
the visual quality of the environment . It promotes water conservation, 
addresses wildfire safety concerns, controls erosion and stormwater 
runoff, manages noxious weeds and invasive plans, and encourages the 
preservation of existing trees and vegetation. Native and/or drought -
tolerant plans are preferred for landscaping. 
 
Irrigation systems may be installed within the Right-of-Way, but they shall 
include features to prevent water from ponding or becoming trapped near 
or under the roadway. The proposed landscaping, irrigation system, 
and/or sleeves must be approved by the Co unty, and a Maintenance 
Agreement must be established with developer to outline their irrigation 
maintenance schedule and responsibilities before any work can 
commence in the County Right -of-Way. The responsible party for 
installing and maintaining all lan dscaping and irrigation in the 
maintenance agreement shall be either the developer, homeowner’s 
association, or property owner. 
 
The review and approval of landscaping plans, as part of an overall 
landscape plan for a development, shall be coordinated with Planning & 
Development Services.

1001 Codes, Ordinances and Standards 
If there is a conflict between the regulations stated in this Chapter and any 
other regulations that apply to the same area, the requirement that is more 
stringent will take precedence. 
 
1001.1 ADOT Roadside Development 
The County has adopted ADOT’s Roadside Development Section 
manuals, guidelines, and details, including but not limited to the following: 
• Stormwater and Erosion/Sediment Control Maps and Manuals 
• Erosion/Sediment and Water Quality Protection Best Management 
Practices (BMP) Details 
• Revegetation and Native Seed Mix Design, Environmental 
Mitigation and Landscape Ecological Design, Native Plant Salvage 
and Replanting 
 
1001.2 Final Stabilization 
In order for an operator of a construction site to submit a Notice of 
Termination (NOT) to the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality 
(ADEQ) or the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, certain 
requirements must be met. These requirements include achi eving final 
stabilization, which is necessary for compliance with the Arizona Pollution 
Discharge Elimination System (AZPDES) Permit or the National Pollutant 
Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Construction General Permit 
(CGP). The AZPDES applies to pro jects that disturb more than one acre 
on non-Tribal Lands. The operator submits a NOT to terminate coverage 
for discharges from construction activities into Waters of the United 
States. For more information on the methodology used by ADOT for 
determining f inal stabilization, refer to ADOT's Methodology for 
Determining Final Stabilization (NOT Criteria). 
 
1002 Preservation of Existing Vegetation 
Wherever feasible, healthy existing trees and shrubs shall be protected in 
place and preserved. These trees and shrubs shall be shown on the 
landscape plan and labeled as “existing to be protected in place.” 
Additionally, they must also be listed on the plant list, including their 
current size. 
 
All landscape plans must identify methods for protecting existing 
vegetation that will remain. Construction materials and debris may not be 
stockpiled within 1½ times the outside drip line perimeter of all trees and

1002.1 Native Plant Salvage and Replanting 
Arizona’s vegetative zones include numerous rare and unique plant 
species, some of which can only be specific geographic areas and are 
limited in numbers. Native plant salvage and replanting on a project must 
be in conformance with the requirements of Arizona Native Plant Laws.  
 
1002.1.1 Non-Discretionary Evaluation Requirements 
• Conformance to requirements of Arizona Native Plant Laws. 
• NEPA Decision Document Requirements. 
• Roadway safety shall not be compromised. 
• Mitigation for 404 permit requirements. 
• Plants must be species that are self -sustaining after planting and 
establishment. 
 
1002.1.2 Discretionary Evaluation Requirements 
• Replanting of salvaged or planting of nursery plant materials would 
maintain or restore wildlife habitat value for cover and movement 
connectivity between habitat areas crossing the roadway. 
• Plant species that exhibit difficulty in regenerating naturally or 
establishing from seeding. 
• Designed replanting quantities should not exceed the area’s 
existing density for individual species and area plant spacing which 
are good indicators of the area’s capacity for sustainable plant 
survival. 
• Maintain or enhance the visual resource quality of the County right-
of-way, professional judgement should be used to achieve an 
appearance similar to the surrounding area and at the same time 
self-sustaining with the available natural moisture. 
• Required maintenance activities would not be affected such as 
ditch and culvert cleaning, mowing, shoulder repair and vegetative 
management and erosion control within a vehicle recovery area. 
• Plants are in good condition with high level of assurance of survival 
and reestablishment. Locations of plants are accessible for 
equipment. 
• Salvage and transplanting of primary or climax vegetation is 
emphasized over transitional or secondary species.

1003 Invasive and Noxious Plant Species 
Refer to the following ADOT-maintained documents to prevent the spread 
of invasive and noxious plants before, during, and after construction: 
• ADOT Invasive and Noxious Plant Species List for Seeds

1004 Seeding Practices for Sustainable Revegetation and 
Erosion Control 
The information in this section is sourced ADOT’s Final Seeding Practices 
PowerPoint. 
 
All disturbed soil areas resulting from construction activities must be 
seeded in order to establish a sustainable native vegetative cover on 
slopes and right-of-way areas. 
 
1004.1 Reasons for Seeding 
 
1004.1.1 Erosion Control 
• Reestablish vegetative cover for erosion protection. 
• Meet Final Stabilization as required by Section 402 of Clean Water 
Act.  
• Minimize long-term maintenance costs. 
 
1004.1.2 Visual and Aesthetic Benefits 
• Successful revegetation with native wildflowers and shrubs 
integrates the aesthetic visual quality of the slopes with the 
surrounding areas. 
• Returns the visual quality of disturbed areas to a natural condition. 
 
1004.1.3 Sustainability 
• Seed mixes include plant species suitable for the native vegetation 
biotic communities.  
• Native grasses, forbs, shrubs, and trees are seeded to establish 
sustainable native plant communities and are vital for habitat 
mitigation and ecological restoration.
